structure.title: Mathematical notation
structure.summary: The text establishes the book's pedagogical approach and mathematical notation, defining conventions for vectors, matrices, transposes, intervals, identity matrices, functionals, asymptotic notation, expectations, conditional expectations, variance, covariance, and data matrices. It then provides the complete contents of a pattern-recognition and machine-learning book, spanning introductory probability, decision and information theory; probability distributions; regression and classification; neural networks; kernel and sparse-kernel methods; graphical models; mixture models and EM; approximate inference; sampling; continuous latent variables; sequential data; and model combination, along with chapter exercises and appendices on data sets, probability distributions, and matrix properties.

nodes.title: 1 Introduction
1.1. Example: Polynomial Curve Fitting
nodes.summary: The text introduces pattern recognition and its supporting theories, then develops polynomial regression as a running example. Noisy samples from sin(2πx) are fitted with polynomials using a closed-form least-squares solution, demonstrating underfitting, over-fitting, generalization, training/test RMS error, the effects of data size and coefficient growth, and model selection. Regularization, including ridge regression and neural-network weight decay, limits coefficient magnitudes and controls effective complexity, while validation sets can tune model order or regularization strength. The discussion concludes by motivating probability theory for representing uncertainty and begins its introduction with a two-box fruit-selection example defining random variables and probability through long-run frequencies.

nodes.title: 1.2. Probability Theory
1.2.1 Probability densities
nodes.summary: The text explains Bayes’ theorem through a fruit-box example, distinguishing prior and posterior probabilities and showing how evidence can reverse an initial preference; it defines independence through factorization of the joint distribution. It then introduces continuous probability densities, interval probabilities, normalization and nonnegativity, cumulative distribution functions, Jacobian-based transformation under changes of variables, and multivariate and mixed distributions. Sum, product, and Bayes rules extend to densities, with marginalization and factorization illustrated for continuous variables. Finally, it defines expectations as probability-weighted sums or integrals and begins discussing their estimation from finite samples.

nodes.title: 1.2.2 Expectations and covariances
nodes.summary: The text develops continuous and mixed probability distributions, including density normalization, probability mass functions, and the sum and product rules, with an informal discretization-based justification. It then defines expectations for discrete and continuous variables, sample-average approximations, variable-specific and conditional expectations, variance and its equivalent formula, and scalar and vector covariance, noting that independent variables have zero covariance.

nodes.title: 1.2.3 Bayesian probabilities
Thomas Bayes
nodes.summary: The text develops the Bayesian view of probability as a rigorous method for quantifying and updating uncertainty, contrasting it with frequentist probability based on repeatable-event frequencies. It motivates probability through coherence axioms, gives historical accounts of Bayes and Laplace, and explains Bayesian inference for model parameters using priors, likelihoods, posteriors, Bayes' theorem, and normalization. It contrasts Bayesian inference with maximum likelihood, frequentist error bars, bootstrap methods, and cross-validation, while discussing the benefits and criticisms of prior distributions. It also reviews computational approaches including Monte Carlo, variational Bayes, and expectation propagation. The section concludes by introducing the Gaussian distribution and its key parameters and properties.

This section presents Bayesian probability as a coherent framework for representing and updating uncertainty, including its historical development and distinction from frequentist probability. It explains priors, likelihoods, posteriors, Bayes' theorem, and normalization in parameter inference; compares Bayesian methods with maximum likelihood and frequentist techniques; considers the benefits and criticisms of priors; surveys Monte Carlo, variational Bayes, and expectation propagation; and concludes with an introduction to the Gaussian distribution and its main properties.

nodes.title: 1.2.4 The Gaussian distribution
nodes.summary: The text discusses the practical development of Bayesian inference through Monte Carlo sampling and deterministic approximations, then introduces the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, their parameters, normalization, moments, variance, and mode. It derives the likelihood for i.i.d. Gaussian data and obtains maximum likelihood estimates for the mean and variance using the log likelihood. It explains that the mean estimate is unbiased while the variance estimate is systematically too small, gives the corrected unbiased estimator, and relates this bias to sample size, overfitting, and the motivation for Bayesian approaches. Finally, it reinterprets polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with a Gaussian centered on the polynomial prediction and parameterized by a precision.

nodes.title: 1.2.5 Curve fitting re-visited
nodes.summary: The text explains the small-sample downward bias of maximum-likelihood Gaussian variance estimates, its reduction with increasing data, and its connection to overfitting in complex models. It then recasts polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with a Gaussian conditional distribution whose mean is the polynomial and whose precision is estimated from residuals. Maximizing the likelihood yields the usual sum-of-squares objective and a predictive Gaussian distribution. Adding a Gaussian prior over coefficients leads, through MAP estimation, to a regularized sum-of-squares objective, while emphasizing that a fully Bayesian treatment would integrate over parameter uncertainty rather than use a single coefficient estimate.

nodes.title: 1.2.6 Bayesian curve fitting
nodes.summary: The text moves from maximum-likelihood polynomial regression to MAP estimation by adding a Gaussian prior over coefficients, showing that MAP is equivalent to regularized least squares. It then presents the fully Bayesian approach, which integrates over parameter uncertainty to produce an analytic Gaussian predictive distribution whose mean and variance depend on the input; the variance reflects both target noise and uncertainty in the model parameters. An illustrative figure shows this predictive distribution. The text concludes by introducing model selection, explaining the roles of model complexity, validation and test sets, overfitting, and cross-validation when data is limited.

This section introduces probability as the foundation for handling uncertainty in pattern recognition, beginning with random variables and a fruit-box example before developing joint, marginal, conditional, sum, product, and Bayes rules. It extends these ideas to discrete, continuous, mixed, and multivariate distributions; transformations; expectations; variance; and covariance. It then presents Bayesian inference, including priors, likelihoods, posteriors, computational methods, and its contrast with frequentist approaches. Gaussian distributions are developed in detail, including parameter estimation and variance bias, and probability is applied to polynomial curve fitting through maximum likelihood, MAP regularization, and fully Bayesian predictive distributions. The section concludes with model selection, overfitting, validation, testing, and cross-validation.

nodes.title: 1.3. Model Selection
nodes.summary: The text introduces model selection after Bayesian polynomial curve fitting, explaining how polynomial order, regularization, and other hyperparameters determine model complexity and should be chosen for generalization performance. It contrasts training, validation, and test sets, describes S-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation for limited data, and notes their computational costs and difficulties with multiple hyperparameters. It then presents information criteria such as AIC, with its likelihood-minus-parameter penalty formula, mentions BIC, and explains their tendency to favor overly simple models because they ignore parameter uncertainty. A fully Bayesian treatment is proposed as a more principled solution, followed by the introduction of the curse of dimensionality.

nodes.title: 1.4. The Curse of Dimensionality
nodes.summary: The text discusses the computational limitations of cross-validation and the shortcomings of AIC/BIC, motivating Bayesian complexity control. It then explains the curse of dimensionality through high-dimensional classification, polynomial parameter growth, cell-count explosion, and the concentration of spherical volume and Gaussian probability in thin shells. Despite these difficulties, lower-dimensional manifolds and local smoothness make high-dimensional pattern recognition feasible. The section concludes by introducing decision theory as the framework for making optimal predictions or actions from probability distributions, illustrated by medical diagnosis.

nodes.title: 1.5. Decision Theory
1.5.1 Minimizing the misclassification rate
nodes.summary: The text introduces decision theory for classification, using Bayes’ theorem to relate priors, likelihoods, joint probabilities, and posterior class probabilities. It shows that minimizing the misclassification rate is achieved by assigning each input to the class with the highest posterior probability, formalized through decision regions and boundaries and generalized from two to K classes. It then explains that classification errors may have unequal consequences, motivating loss matrices and expected-loss minimization. The optimal decision assigns each input to the class or action with the lowest posterior expected loss, illustrated by an asymmetric cancer-diagnosis cost matrix.

nodes.title: 1.5.2 Minimizing the expected loss
nodes.summary: The text explains decision-making in classification when errors have unequal consequences. It introduces loss matrices and expected-loss minimization, deriving the rule of assigning each input to the class with the smallest posterior expected loss. It then presents the reject option, in which uncertain inputs are withheld based on a posterior-probability threshold, and notes how rejection can also be incorporated into loss minimization. Finally, it begins distinguishing inference, which estimates posterior class probabilities from training data, from decision, which uses them for classification.

nodes.title: 1.5.3 The reject option
nodes.summary: The text explains loss-based classification and the reject option. Inputs are assigned to the class with minimum expected loss using posterior probabilities and a loss matrix. Because errors arise in regions of posterior uncertainty, a threshold-based reject option can defer ambiguous cases, potentially to a human expert. The threshold determines the rejection rate, with extreme settings guaranteeing all or no rejections, and the criterion can incorporate rejection loss. Classification is framed as separate inference and decision stages, beginning with learning p(C_k|x) from training data.

nodes.title: 1.5.4 Inference and decision
nodes.summary: The text explains decision theory for classification and regression. Classification decisions minimize expected loss using posterior probabilities, while a reject option with threshold θ allows uncertain inputs to be deferred and can be optimized under a loss matrix. It contrasts generative models, which learn class-conditional densities and priors, discriminative posterior models, and direct discriminant functions, discussing their complexity, data requirements, novelty-detection capability, and loss of probability information. Posterior probabilities support changing loss criteria, rejection, correction for class-prior changes caused by balanced training data, and systematic combination of separate information sources through conditional independence and naive Bayes. The text then introduces regression loss functions, defines expected loss, and shows that squared-error loss is minimized by predicting the conditional mean of the target given the input.

nodes.title: 1.5.5 Loss functions for regression
nodes.summary: The text explains naive Bayes classification through conditional independence of multiple observations, posterior computation, class priors, normalization, and limitations of marginal factorization. It then develops regression decision theory, showing that squared-error minimization produces the conditional-mean regression function, decomposes error into reducible prediction error and irreducible noise, and presents three modeling approaches. It generalizes squared loss through Minkowski loss, whose optimal predictions range from mean to median to mode. Finally, it introduces information theory, characterizing information as probability-dependent surprise that is additive for independent events and therefore logarithmic in probability.

This section introduces decision theory as the process of converting probabilistic inference into optimal predictions or actions under uncertainty. It develops Bayesian classification using posterior probabilities, decision regions, unequal-error loss matrices, expected-loss minimization, and rejection of ambiguous cases. It distinguishes inference from decision and compares generative, discriminative, and direct classification approaches, including naive Bayes, prior correction, novelty detection, and combining independent evidence. It then treats regression, showing how different loss functions determine optimal predictions—especially the conditional mean under squared loss—and separates reducible prediction error from irreducible noise. The section concludes by generalizing regression losses from mean to median and mode predictions and introducing probability-based information measures.

nodes.title: 1.6. Information Theory
Ludwig Boltzmann
nodes.summary: The text develops continuous information theory by defining differential entropy as the continuous limit of discrete entropy, explaining its divergent discretization offset, and finding that the maximum-entropy continuous distribution with fixed mean and variance is Gaussian. It derives the Gaussian entropy and notes that differential entropy may be negative. It then defines conditional entropy and the chain rule, introduces relative entropy/Kullback–Leibler divergence as the coding penalty for using an approximate distribution, notes its asymmetry and nonnegativity, and begins a convexity-based proof of these properties. Historical sidebars discuss Boltzmann’s statistical interpretation of thermodynamic entropy and Shannon’s foundational contributions to information theory.

It then presents five exercises covering derivation of the normal equations for polynomial least-squares fitting, formulation of the corresponding regularized equations, a discrete probability and Bayes problem involving coloured boxes and fruit, the effect of nonlinear and linear variable transformations on probability-density maxima, and verification of a variance identity for a function f(x).

nodes.summary: Exercises 1.6–1.11 cover covariance under independence, evaluation and normalization of the Gaussian integral, verification of Gaussian moment and normalization identities, identification of Gaussian modes, mean and variance of sums of independent variables, and derivation of Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimates for the mean and variance.

nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.12–1.41 covering Gaussian moments and unbiased variance estimation; symmetric and antisymmetric matrices; counting coefficients in multivariate polynomials and their asymptotic growth; gamma functions and hypersphere geometry; high-dimensional volume and Gaussian concentration; Bayesian classification, general losses, rejection, and error bounds; conditional means, medians, and modes for regression; entropy, Jensen's inequality, KL divergence, mutual information, independence, transformations, and deterministic dependence; maximum-entropy derivation of the Gaussian; convexity; and numerical entropy calculations for a binary joint distribution.

This section introduces information theory through conditional entropy, relative entropy, convexity and Jensen’s inequality, and mutual information, linking these concepts to coding efficiency, density estimation, likelihood maximization, and statistical independence. It also highlights Claude Shannon’s contributions and provides exercises spanning Gaussian analysis, probability, estimation, linear algebra, geometry, high-dimensional behavior, Bayesian decision theory, regression, entropy, divergences, transformations, and maximum-entropy principles.

This section introduces Claude Shannon’s information theory through conditional and relative entropy, convexity and Jensen’s inequality, and mutual information, relating them to coding, density estimation, likelihood methods, and independence. It also provides exercises covering probability, Gaussian models, estimation, linear algebra, geometry, high-dimensional phenomena, Bayesian decision theory, regression, entropy, divergences, transformations, and maximum-entropy methods.

The section introduces information theory for machine learning, beginning with information content, entropy, units, coding efficiency, and Shannon’s noiseless coding theorem, then connecting entropy to thermodynamic disorder and Boltzmann’s work. It extends these ideas to continuous variables through differential entropy and the Gaussian maximum-entropy result, develops conditional entropy and the chain rule, and defines relative entropy/Kullback–Leibler divergence and mutual information, including their coding, convexity, nonnegativity, asymmetry, independence, density-estimation, likelihood, and transformation interpretations. Historical notes on Boltzmann and Shannon and a broad set of related exercises complete the section.

This section introduces pattern recognition and machine learning through handwritten-digit recognition, emphasizing adaptive models, training and test data, generalization, preprocessing, feature extraction, and the distinction between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. It develops polynomial curve fitting to illustrate estimation, noise, underfitting, overfitting, regularization, validation, and probabilistic prediction, then establishes probability theory and Bayesian inference as frameworks for uncertainty, distributions, Gaussian models, likelihood, MAP estimation, and Bayesian prediction. It explains model selection using validation, cross-validation, information criteria, and Bayesian complexity control; examines the curse of dimensionality and why structure such as manifolds and local smoothness helps; and introduces decision theory for optimal classification and regression under loss. Finally, it presents information theory, including entropy, coding, differential entropy, KL divergence, and mutual information, along with their mathematical, statistical, and machine-learning interpretations.

nodes.title: 2 Probability Distributions
2.1. Binary Variables
2.1.1 The beta distribution
nodes.summary: This section derives the mean and variance of the binomial distribution, introduces the normalized beta distribution as a conjugate prior for Bernoulli/binomial parameters, and derives its moments and beta-form posterior after observing successes and failures. It explains hyperparameters as effective prior observations, sequential Bayesian updating, predictive probabilities, convergence to maximum likelihood with large data sets, and posterior concentration. It then gives general identities relating prior and average posterior means and variances, showing that uncertainty decreases on average but not necessarily for every data set, before beginning the introduction of multinomial variables and their 1-of-K representation.

This section develops the modeling and inference of binary outcomes. It defines the Bernoulli distribution and its moments, derives likelihood-based estimation and the sufficient statistic, and introduces the binomial distribution for counts of successes. It then addresses maximum-likelihood overfitting through Bayesian inference with the beta conjugate prior, deriving posterior moments, effective-prior-count interpretations, sequential updating, predictive probabilities, large-sample convergence, and posterior uncertainty properties, before beginning the treatment of multinomial variables.

nodes.title: 2.2. Multinomial Variables
2.2.1 The Dirichlet distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the multinomial maximum-likelihood estimate and distribution for category counts, then introduces the Dirichlet distribution as the multinomial’s conjugate prior, including its simplex support, normalization, posterior update, effective-count interpretation, and illustrative plots. It also notes the relationship between binomial/beta and two-category multinomial/Dirichlet models, provides a biographical sidebar on Dirichlet, and begins the section on univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, motivating them through maximum entropy and the central limit theorem.

The section reviews how Bayesian uncertainty changes with data, then introduces multinomial variables in 1-of-K form, derives their distribution, moments, likelihood, sufficient statistics, and maximum-likelihood setup. It proceeds to the Dirichlet conjugate prior, its normalization and posterior interpretation, connects it to the beta distribution, includes background material on Dirichlet, and begins the transition to Gaussian distributions motivated by maximum entropy and the central limit theorem.

nodes.title: 2.3. The Gaussian Distribution
nodes.summary: The text transitions from Dirichlet and binary/multinomial representations to an introduction of the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, giving their parameterized formulas and explaining their roles as maximum-entropy distributions and as limiting distributions under the central limit theorem. A uniform-variable averaging example and the Gaussian approximation to the binomial are noted, followed by an indication that the section will develop Gaussian geometry and analytical methods using matrix identities. It also includes a biographical sidebar on Carl Friedrich Gauss and his mathematical and scientific contributions.

This section introduces probability distributions as building blocks for pattern-recognition models and as settings for studying density estimation and Bayesian inference under an i.i.d. assumption. It develops Bernoulli, binomial, multinomial, beta, and Dirichlet models, covering their moments, likelihoods, sufficient statistics, estimation, conjugate Bayesian updating, prediction, uncertainty, and asymptotic behavior. It then introduces univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, explaining their maximum-entropy and central-limit-theorem foundations, Gaussian approximations, and forthcoming geometric and matrix-based analysis, alongside a biographical note on Carl Friedrich Gauss.

nodes.title: Appendix C
Carl Friedrich Gauss
nodes.summary: This section explains why Gaussian distributions arise from averaging and from large-sample binomial behavior, then develops their geometry, normalization, and moments. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues transform the distribution into independent coordinates, revealing ellipsoidal constant-density surfaces, the role of the Mahalanobis distance, and the requirements for positive definiteness. It establishes that μ and Σ are respectively the mean and covariance, discusses parameter-count and modeling limitations of general, diagonal, and isotropic covariance forms, and describes latent-variable and structured-model solutions. Finally, it introduces conditional Gaussian distributions, partitioned covariance and precision matrices, and the setup for deriving Gaussian conditionals.

nodes.title: 2.3.1 Conditional Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text develops the conditional distribution of one subset of variables in a multivariate Gaussian after partitioning the vector, mean, covariance, and precision matrix. By expanding the Gaussian quadratic form and completing the square, it derives the conditional covariance and mean in terms of precision blocks, then uses a partitioned-matrix inverse and Schur complement identity to express them in terms of covariance blocks. The conditional distribution is Gaussian, with a mean linear in the conditioned variables and covariance independent of them, providing an example of a linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 2.3.2 Marginal Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal of a partitioned joint Gaussian by completing the square and integrating out one subvect​or. It finds that the marginal remains Gaussian with mean μ_a and covariance (Λ_aa − Λ_abΛ_bb^{-1}Λ_ba)^{-1} = Σ_aa, and explains the contrast between covariance-based marginal formulas and precision-based conditional formulas. It summarizes the conditional and marginal Gaussian distributions, illustrates them graphically, and then introduces Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables with a Gaussian marginal and a linear-mean, x-independent-covariance conditional.

nodes.title: 2.3.3 Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables
nodes.summary: The text reviews conditional and marginal distributions of partitioned multivariate Gaussians, illustrated by a two-variable example, then derives Bayes’ theorem for a linear Gaussian model. It obtains the joint precision, covariance, and mean, followed by the Gaussian marginal p(y) and posterior conditional p(x|y), including the Gaussian-convolution special case and prior/posterior interpretation. It concludes with maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian, identifying the sufficient statistics and deriving the sample mean as the maximum-likelihood estimate of the mean.

nodes.title: 2.3.4 Maximum likelihood for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal and conditional distributions associated with Gaussian variables, then develops maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian. It identifies the sufficient statistics, derives the sample-mean and sample-covariance estimators, analyzes their expectations and the covariance estimator’s bias, and presents the unbiased covariance correction. It concludes by introducing sequential maximum-likelihood estimation for processing observations incrementally in online or large-data settings.

nodes.title: 2.3.5 Sequential estimation
nodes.summary: The text derives the multivariate Gaussian maximum-likelihood covariance estimator, establishes that the mean estimate is unbiased but the covariance estimate is biased by a factor of (N-1)/N, and gives the corresponding unbiased correction. It then introduces sequential estimation, showing the recursive sample-mean update and developing the Robbins–Monro procedure for finding roots of regression functions under step-size and variance conditions. Maximum-likelihood estimation is expressed as a root-finding problem using the expected score, with the Gaussian mean as a concrete example that recovers the sequential mean update and generalizes to multiple variables. Finally, it opens the Bayesian treatment of Gaussian parameters by considering an unknown mean with known variance and presenting the resulting likelihood and motivation for a Gaussian prior.

nodes.title: 2.3.6 Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of Gaussian sequential mean estimation and introduces Bayesian Gaussian inference. It derives the Gaussian posterior for an unknown mean with known variance, explains its precision-weighted mean, limiting behavior, graphical illustration, and sequential interpretation. It then derives the gamma posterior for unknown precision with known mean, including effective prior observations and the inverse-gamma alternative. For jointly unknown mean and precision, it presents the normal-gamma conjugate prior and extends the results to multivariate Gaussians using Gaussian, Wishart, and normal-Wishart priors. The section concludes by introducing Student's t-distribution as the result of marginalizing a Gaussian's precision under a gamma prior.

nodes.title: 2.3.7 Student’s t-distribution
nodes.summary: The text presents multivariate Gaussian conjugate priors, including the Wishart, inverse Wishart, and normal-Wishart distributions. It derives Student’s t-distribution by integrating a Gaussian’s gamma-distributed precision, explains its parameterization, limiting cases, scale-mixture interpretation, heavy tails, robustness to outliers, and multivariate extension with its moments and Mahalanobis-distance form. It then introduces periodic variables, explains why ordinary Gaussian modeling is origin-dependent, and begins an invariant circular-mean approach based on averaging unit vectors.

nodes.title: 2.3.8 Periodic variables
nodes.summary: The text first gives the multivariate Student’s t-distribution and its mean, covariance, and mode. It then explains why ordinary Gaussians are unsuitable for periodic variables, develops the invariant circular mean using unit vectors, and derives the von Mises distribution by conditioning an isotropic two-dimensional Gaussian on the unit circle. It defines the von Mises normalization through a Bessel function, interprets its parameters, gives its large-concentration Gaussian approximation, and derives maximum-likelihood estimates for direction and concentration. Alternative periodic modeling strategies and mixtures of von Mises distributions are outlined. Finally, the text introduces Gaussian mixtures through the Old Faithful example, showing how mixtures capture multimodal data better than a single Gaussian.

nodes.title: 2.3.9 Mixtures of Gaussians
nodes.summary: The text moves from periodic-distribution alternatives and the multimodal extension of the von Mises distribution to Gaussian mixture models. It uses the bimodal Old Faithful data and figures to motivate mixtures, defines Gaussian mixtures and their constraints, explains their latent-component interpretation and posterior responsibilities, and notes that their maximum-likelihood parameters require numerical optimization or expectation maximization. It then introduces the exponential family, its normalized general form and natural parameters, and demonstrates that the Bernoulli distribution is an exponential-family member.

nodes.title: 2.4. The Exponential Family
2.4.1 Maximum likelihood and sufficient statistics
nodes.summary: The text introduces the Gaussian as an exponential-family distribution and develops maximum likelihood, sufficient statistics, conjugate priors, and the beginning of noninformative-prior theory for general exponential-family models. Differentiating the normalization function yields moments, while maximum likelihood depends only on summed sufficient statistics and becomes exact asymptotically. Conjugate priors preserve the exponential-family form after observing data and can be interpreted through pseudo-observations; the text then begins discussing how prior knowledge and zero-probability assignments affect posterior distributions.

nodes.title: 2.4.2 Conjugate priors
nodes.summary: The text explains that exponential-family maximum-likelihood estimation depends on data only through sufficient statistics, gives Bernoulli and Gaussian examples, and notes that the estimator converges to the true parameter as the sample size grows, with sufficiency also applying to Bayesian inference. It then defines conjugate priors for exponential-family distributions, derives the same-form posterior and its updated parameters, and interprets the prior-strength parameter as a number of pseudo-observations. Finally, it introduces noninformative priors and notes that posterior distributions retain any zero-probability exclusions imposed by the prior.

nodes.title: 2.4.3 Noninformative priors
nodes.summary: The text explains sufficient statistics in exponential-family maximum likelihood, including examples and asymptotic recovery of the true parameter, and notes that sufficiency also applies to Bayesian inference. It derives the general conjugate prior for exponential-family models, shows that the posterior retains the prior's form, and interprets the prior strength as pseudo-observations. It then discusses noninformative priors, including improper priors, posterior propriety, parameterization dependence, and invariant priors for location and scale parameters, with Gaussian mean, standard deviation, and precision examples. Finally, it introduces nonparametric density estimation as an alternative to restrictive parametric models and describes histogram density estimation and its normalization.

This section introduces the exponential family, its normalized representation, natural parameters, and sufficient statistics, and demonstrates the form for Bernoulli, multinomial, and Gaussian distributions, including sigmoid and softmax parameterizations and multinomial constraints. It develops the role of sufficient statistics in maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, derives conjugate priors and posterior updates with a pseudo-observation interpretation, and discusses noninformative and improper priors, posterior propriety, parameterization and invariance issues, and Gaussian location-scale examples. It concludes by introducing nonparametric histogram density estimation, while noting that Gaussian-mixture likelihoods require numerical optimization or expectation maximization.

nodes.title: 2.5. Nonparametric Methods
2.5.1 Kernel density estimators
nodes.summary: The text develops local nonparametric density estimation from binomial counting arguments, deriving the estimate p(x) approximately K/(NV) and explaining its competing locality and sample-size requirements. It distinguishes kernel estimation, which fixes region volume, from nearest-neighbour estimation, which fixes the number of enclosed points, noting their convergence under suitable scaling. Kernel estimators are constructed first with a hypercube Parzen window and then with smooth Gaussian kernels, whose bandwidth controls the trade-off between noise and over-smoothing. Valid kernels must be nonnegative and normalized. These estimators have no training computation beyond data storage but require evaluation time linear in dataset size. The section then motivates nearest-neighbour methods as an adaptive alternative for densities that vary across space and begins their construction using a fixed point count and a data-determined spherical volume.

nodes.title: 2.5.2 Nearest-neighbour methods
nodes.summary: The text compares kernel and nearest-neighbour nonparametric density estimation. Kernel density estimation uses a bandwidth h as a smoothing and complexity parameter, with an intermediate value balancing noise and oversmoothing; valid kernels must be nonnegative and normalized. Parzen estimators require only storage during training but become increasingly expensive to evaluate as the data set grows. K-nearest-neighbour density estimation instead adapts the neighbourhood volume to contain a fixed number K of points, with K controlling smoothing, though the resulting estimate is not a proper globally integrable density. Applying this method class by class and Bayes’ theorem yields K-nearest-neighbour classification, which assigns a point by majority vote among its K nearest training examples; K = 1 is the nearest-neighbour rule. Figures illustrate density smoothing, decision boundaries, and oil-flow classifications for different K values. The nearest-neighbour asymptotic error is bounded by twice the optimal error, while tree structures can reduce search costs. The section concludes that later methods must combine the flexibility of nonparametric models with complexity control independent of training-set size. The exercises cover Bernoulli moments and entropy, an alternative {-1,1} Bernoulli representation, and the normalization proof for the binomial distribution.

The section introduces nonparametric methods as flexible alternatives to restrictive parametric density models. It covers histogram estimation and its normalization, bin-width trade-offs, practical advantages, discontinuities, and curse-of-dimensionality limitations. It then develops local density estimation through Parzen and smooth kernel estimators, explaining neighborhood volume, sample-size requirements, kernel validity, bandwidth selection, computational costs, and convergence. Nearest-neighbour methods are presented as adaptive alternatives using neighborhoods containing a fixed number of points, including their use in K-nearest-neighbour classification, smoothing and decision-boundary behavior, asymptotic error guarantees, and tree-based acceleration. The section concludes by motivating complexity-controlled flexible models and lists exercises on Bernoulli distributions, entropy, alternative coding, and binomial normalization.

It then presents exercises on verifying Bernoulli normalization, moments, and entropy; analyzing the equivalent ±1 Bernoulli representation; and proving binomial normalization using a combinatorial identity.

It then presents Exercises 2.1–2.6, covering the properties and entropy of Bernoulli distributions in two parameterizations, proofs of the binomial theorem and binomial normalization, derivations of binomial mean and variance, proof of beta-distribution normalization from gamma integrals, and derivation of the beta distribution's mean, variance, and mode.

nodes.title: 3 Linear Models for Regression
3.1. Linear Basis Function Models
3.1.1 Maximum likelihood and least squares
nodes.summary: The text develops linear basis-function regression from Gaussian-noise assumptions, covering basis-function choices, likelihood and log-likelihood derivations, the equivalence of maximum likelihood and least squares, normal equations, the design matrix and pseudo-inverse, interpretation of the bias and noise precision, and the geometric projection view of least squares. It also discusses multimodal-distribution limitations of Gaussian noise, numerical instability from nearly dependent basis functions and remedies using SVD or regularization, and motivates sequential learning for large data sets.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Geometry of least squares
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of least squares: target values and basis functions are vectors in an N-dimensional space, predictions lie in the subspace spanned by the basis vectors, and minimizing squared error corresponds to orthogonally projecting the target vector onto that subspace. It notes that inverse noise precision is the residual variance. It also discusses numerical problems with nearly singular design matrices caused by collinear basis functions, recommending SVD and noting that regularization prevents singularity. Finally, it introduces sequential (online) learning as a computationally efficient alternative to batch processing for large data sets.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Sequential learning
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of least squares as the orthogonal projection of the target vector onto the subspace spanned by basis-function vectors, while noting that residual variance determines inverse noise precision. It discusses numerical instability in normal-equation solutions caused by nearly dependent basis functions and remedies such as SVD and regularization. It then introduces sequential learning for large or streaming data sets, derives stochastic gradient descent and the LMS update, and emphasizes careful learning-rate selection. Finally, it presents regularized least squares, including the quadratic weight-decay penalty, which controls overfitting by shrinking unsupported weights toward zero.

nodes.title: 3.1.4 Regularized least squares
nodes.summary: The text introduces sequential stochastic-gradient learning and the LMS update, then develops regularized least squares. Quadratic regularization yields weight decay, parameter shrinkage, and a closed-form ridge solution; generalized |w_j|^q penalties include the lasso, whose constrained geometry can produce sparse models. Regularization controls over-fitting by limiting effective complexity but requires selecting λ. The section then extends linear basis-function regression to multiple outputs using a shared basis-function matrix, an isotropic Gaussian target distribution, and its corresponding matrix-form log likelihood.

nodes.title: 3.1.5 Multiple outputs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of regularization by contrasting quadratic and lasso constraints, noting the lasso's sparse solutions and motivating a focus on quadratic regularization. It then extends linear regression to multiple target variables using a shared basis-function matrix and a matrix of parameters under isotropic Gaussian noise. Maximum likelihood yields a matrix least-squares solution, with each target solved independently using a common pseudoinverse; this decoupling also holds for general Gaussian covariance structures. The text subsequently introduces the bias-variance decomposition, explaining overfitting, the flexibility-versus-complexity trade-off, the limitations of selecting regularization by direct minimization, and the motivation for comparing frequentist bias-variance analysis with Bayesian treatment of model complexity.

This section introduces linear regression and linear basis-function models, emphasizing that they are linear in their parameters even when nonlinear in the inputs. It presents common basis functions and their uses, then derives Gaussian-noise maximum likelihood as least squares, including normal-equation, pseudoinverse, geometric projection, and noise-variance interpretations. It addresses numerical instability and large-data computation through SVD, regularization, and sequential stochastic-gradient or LMS learning. Regularized least squares is developed through weight decay, ridge regression, and generalized penalties such as the sparse lasso, explaining its role in controlling overfitting. The treatment is extended to multiple target variables with matrix formulations and Gaussian noise, and concludes with bias-variance analysis, model flexibility, complexity selection, and motivation for Bayesian approaches.

nodes.title: 3.2. The Bias-Variance Decomposition
nodes.summary: The text first derives the multivariate linear-regression maximum-likelihood solution, showing that target variables decouple and share a design-matrix pseudoinverse, including under general Gaussian noise covariance. It then introduces the frequentist bias-variance decomposition of expected squared prediction loss into squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise, explains the meanings and opposing behavior of bias and variance under model complexity and regularization, and illustrates the trade-off with sinusoidal data fitted using Gaussian basis functions. Empirical bias, variance, and test-error estimates identify an intermediate regularization level, but the approach is limited in practice because it requires an ensemble of data sets. The text therefore motivates Bayesian linear regression as a way to address overfitting and infer model complexity from training data, beginning with a Gaussian conjugate prior over weights with known noise precision.

nodes.title: 3.3. Bayesian Linear Regression
3.3.1 Parameter distribution
nodes.summary: The text moves from the limitations of the frequentist bias-variance view and regularization trade-off to Bayesian linear regression as a principled way to control overfitting and infer model complexity from training data. It derives Gaussian priors and posteriors for linear models, explains MAP, maximum-likelihood and sequential-update special cases, and relates the Gaussian prior to quadratic regularization. A straight-line synthetic-data example illustrates how likelihoods and posterior distributions become more concentrated as observations accumulate. It also discusses non-Gaussian exponential-power priors and their corresponding regularization effects. Finally, it derives the Gaussian predictive distribution, showing that predictive uncertainty combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty, the latter decreasing as more data are observed and vanishing asymptotically.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text generalizes the weight prior beyond the Gaussian case, relating posterior maximization to regularized regression and noting the special conjugacy and mode-mean equality of q = 2. It derives the Gaussian predictive distribution for Bayesian linear regression, including its mean and additive noise-plus-parameter-uncertainty variance, and explains how uncertainty changes with data quantity and input location. Examples using noisy sinusoidal data illustrate predictive means, pointwise uncertainty, and posterior-function samples. It discusses the undesirable overconfidence of localized-basis models during extrapolation, Gaussian-process regression as an alternative, and the Student's t predictive distribution obtained when both weights and noise precision are unknown. Finally, it introduces the equivalent kernel interpretation, showing that predictions are weighted combinations of training targets with generally stronger weights for nearby inputs.

nodes.title: 3.3.3 Equivalent kernel
nodes.summary: The text explains the equivalent kernel in Bayesian linear regression: the predictive mean is a data-dependent weighted sum of training targets, with weights typically localized near the query point, and the kernel also determines correlations and joint predictive uncertainty. This motivates defining kernels directly and leads to Gaussian processes. The weights sum to one under specified basis-function conditions but may be negative, and the kernel has an inner-product representation. The text then introduces Bayesian model comparison, emphasizing parameter marginalization as protection against overfitting and as a way to compare models directly using all training data, with posterior model probabilities determined by model priors and the data evidence.

This section develops Bayesian linear regression from its motivation in overfitting control and regularization through Gaussian and non-Gaussian priors, posterior inference, MAP and maximum-likelihood special cases, and sequential updating. It derives predictive distributions and explains how noise and parameter uncertainty vary with data quantity and input location, illustrating these ideas with synthetic line and sinusoidal examples and discussing Student’s t predictions and Gaussian-process alternatives. It then interprets predictions through the equivalent kernel as weighted combinations of training targets, covering its localization, uncertainty and correlation properties, weight behavior, and inner-product form, before introducing Bayesian model comparison based on parameter marginalization, model priors, and data evidence.

nodes.title: 3.4. Bayesian Model Comparison
nodes.summary: The text concludes the equivalent-kernel discussion by noting that kernel weights may be negative and that the kernel has an inner-product feature representation. It then introduces Bayesian model comparison as a way to control overfitting by integrating over parameters, defining posterior model probabilities through priors and model evidence, and combining model predictions through posterior-weighted averaging. Evidence is the parameter-marginalized likelihood and supports Bayes factors; a peak-width approximation reveals a trade-off between data fit and a complexity penalty that grows with parameter count. Generative data-set distributions explain why intermediate-complexity models may be preferred, while expected Bayes factors favor the true model when it is included among the candidates. The approach depends on appropriate, proper priors and model assumptions, so an independent test set remains useful. Finally, the evidence approximation for linear regression is presented: rather than fully integrating over weights and hyperparameters, it fixes α and β at marginal-likelihood-maximizing values and integrates over the weights, approximating full Bayesian prediction when the hyperparameter posterior is sharply concentrated.

nodes.title: 3.5. The Evidence Approximation
3.5.1 Evaluation of the evidence function
nodes.summary: This text introduces Bayesian evidence optimization for the hyperparameters α and β in linear regression, explaining its relation to regularization, alternatives involving Gamma priors and Laplace or EM methods, and the superiority of evidence maximization over Laplace approximation in skewed cases. It derives the marginal likelihood by completing the square in the weight vector, identifies the Hessian and posterior mean, evaluates the Gaussian integral, and obtains the log-evidence formula. A polynomial-regression example shows how evidence balances fit and complexity and selects a cubic model. Finally, it begins maximizing the evidence with respect to α using the eigenvalues of βΦᵀΦ and derives the corresponding stationary-point equation.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Maximizing the evidence function
nodes.summary: The passage explains why Bayesian model evidence selects a cubic polynomial over both simpler and more complex models, balancing fit improvement against complexity. It then derives iterative evidence-maximization updates for the prior precision α and noise precision β using the eigenvalues of βΦᵀΦ, the posterior mode, and the effective parameter count γ. It explains that γ measures how many parameter directions are actually determined by the data, illustrates prior-induced shrinkage in eigenvector-aligned parameter space, and shows how the Bayesian variance estimate uses N − γ rather than N degrees of freedom.

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Effective number of parameters
nodes.summary: The section explains the effective number of parameters in Bayesian linear regression through the eigenvalues of the likelihood Hessian: α suppresses weakly determined parameter directions while preserving well-determined ones, and γ quantifies the resulting effective model complexity. This quantity corrects the Bayesian noise-variance estimate by replacing N with N−γ, generalizing the usual degrees-of-freedom correction. A sinusoidal Gaussian-basis example shows how evidence selects α, aligns with the evidence maximum and good generalization, and controls parameter magnitudes. In the large-data limit γ=M, yielding simplified hyperparameter updates, after which the text introduces limitations of models using fixed basis functions.

This section presents the evidence approximation for Bayesian linear regression: instead of fully marginalizing over weights and hyperparameters, it integrates over the weights and chooses the prior and noise precisions α and β by maximizing the marginal likelihood. It derives the evidence and its optimization updates, relates the method to regularization and alternative empirical-Bayes procedures, and shows how evidence balances fit against complexity in selecting models such as a cubic polynomial. The effective parameter count γ explains prior-induced shrinkage, corrects variance estimation through N−γ degrees of freedom, and yields simplified large-data updates. Examples with polynomial and sinusoidal Gaussian-basis models illustrate model selection, generalization, and parameter control, while the section also notes the sensitivity of evidence to prior assumptions, the problems with improper priors, the possible use of evidence ratios or test data, and limitations of fixed-basis models.

nodes.title: 3.6. Limitations of Fixed Basis Functions
nodes.summary: The passage interprets evidence-based regularization through two figures, showing that the optimum hyperparameter is identified by the intersection of γ and 2αE_W and coincides with the evidence maximum and near-optimal generalization, while noting that the formulas avoid Hessian eigenvalue calculations. It then shows how Gaussian-model weights vary with effective model complexity. The section explains both the strengths and limitations of fixed-basis linear regression: although it offers closed-form estimation, tractable Bayesian methods, and flexible nonlinear mappings, fixed bases suffer from the curse of dimensionality and may require exponentially many functions. Lower-dimensional data manifolds, localized bases, adaptive neural-network bases, and learned relevant directions help address these problems. The passage concludes with an exercise proving the logistic–tanh identity and deriving the parameter conversion between the two basis-function representations.

nodes.title: 3.1 ( ) www

It also notes that neural networks can identify the few input directions relevant to targets. The exercise establishes the mathematical equivalence between logistic sigmoid and tanh functions and asks for the resulting parameter transformation between the two corresponding linear models.
