This section introduces linear regression for continuous-target prediction and develops fixed-basis models that are linear in their parameters but potentially nonlinear in their inputs. It covers least-squares and maximum-likelihood estimation, geometric and matrix formulations, numerical methods, multivariate targets, regularization, and bias-variance analysis. It then develops Bayesian linear regression, including priors, posterior and predictive inference, sequential learning, uncertainty, Student’s t distributions, equivalent kernels, and Gaussian-process connections. Bayesian model comparison and the evidence approximation are presented as methods for balancing data fit, parameter uncertainty, and model complexity, with effective parameter counts, hyperparameter updates, and practical limitations. The section concludes by examining the curse of dimensionality and adaptive alternatives to fixed bases, and provides exercises spanning regression geometry, weighted and regularized least squares, multivariate and Bayesian inference, predictive distributions, equivalent kernels, evidence calculations, and sigmoid–tanh basis equivalence.

nodes.title: 4 Linear Models for Classification
4.1. Discriminant Functions
4.1.1 Two classes
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear discriminant functions for classification, noting their nonlinear dependence on parameters in the broader model context and the applicability of fixed basis-function transformations. It defines two-class linear discriminants, explains how the weight vector and bias determine the orientation and position of the hyperplane decision boundary, derives the signed-distance interpretation of the discriminant, and presents augmented-vector notation. It then begins the discussion of multiclass classification, warning that combining binary classifiers—such as one-versus-the-rest models—creates difficulties.

nodes.title: 4.1.2 Multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometry and signed-distance interpretation of binary linear discriminants, including an augmented-vector representation. It then examines multiclass classification, showing why one-versus-the-rest and one-versus-one combinations can produce ambiguous regions, and presents a unified K-function discriminant whose pairwise boundaries are hyperplanes and whose decision regions are convex and singly connected. Finally, it introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as learning methods, beginning with least-squares classification using 1-of-K targets and noting its imperfect interpretation as posterior probabilities.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Least squares for classification
nodes.summary: The text proves that multiclass linear-discriminant decision regions are singly connected and convex, notes the equivalence of the two-class and single-discriminant formulations, and introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as methods for learning linear classifiers. It develops the least-squares classifier for 1-of-K targets, including its matrix formulation, closed-form pseudoinverse solution, and output-sum constraint. It explains why these outputs are not generally probabilities and illustrates major weaknesses of least squares—outlier sensitivity, penalization of overly confident correct predictions, and poor multiclass boundaries—attributing them to the inappropriate Gaussian assumption before beginning the discussion of Fisher’s linear discriminant.

nodes.title: 4.1.4 Fisher’s linear discriminant
nodes.summary: The text discusses the limitations of least-squares classification, including sensitivity to outliers and poor multiclass performance caused by its inappropriate Gaussian assumption for discrete targets. It then introduces Fisher’s linear discriminant as a dimensionality-reduction approach: project data onto a one-dimensional direction and choose the direction that maximizes between-class separation relative to within-class variance. The resulting direction is proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 − m_1), reducing to the difference of class means for isotropic within-class covariance. A threshold can be applied to the projection, with Gaussian class models providing one way to determine it. The section concludes by introducing the relationship between Fisher’s criterion and least-squares classification under alternative target coding.

nodes.title: 4.1.5 Relation to least squares
nodes.summary: The text derives Fisher’s linear discriminant by maximizing the ratio of between-class to within-class variance, obtaining the projection direction w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1). It explains the isotropic-covariance special case, distinguishes the projection from the subsequent threshold-based classifier, and discusses Gaussian modeling of projected classes and threshold selection. It then shows that, for two classes, Fisher’s direction is recovered from least squares by using targets N/N1 and -N/N2, derives the corresponding bias w0 = -w^T m, and concludes that classification can be performed using y(x) = w^T(x - m), assigning points with positive output to C1 and the remainder to C2.

nodes.title: 4.1.6 Fisher’s discriminant for multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text generalizes Fisher’s discriminant analysis from two to K classes by projecting inputs into multiple linear features, defining within-class, total, and between-class covariance matrices in both the original and projected spaces, and optimizing a trace criterion that favors large between-class and small within-class covariance. The optimal projection uses leading generalized eigenvectors, but no more than K − 1 useful features can be obtained because the between-class covariance has rank at most K − 1. It then introduces the perceptron as a two-class linear discriminant that applies a fixed nonlinear feature transformation before a generalized linear model.

nodes.title: 4.1.7 The perceptron algorithm
Frank Rosenblatt
nodes.summary: The text explains the perceptron’s step activation, bias feature, ±1 target coding, perceptron criterion, and stochastic-gradient learning rule. It discusses why direct misclassification-count minimization is unsuitable, how updates affect individual and total errors, and the convergence theorem and its limitations for separable and nonseparable data. It also covers perceptron history through Frank Rosenblatt, Minsky and Papert’s criticism and its impact, illustrations of algorithmic convergence and early hardware, the model’s lack of probabilistic and multiclass capabilities and its fixed-basis linear limitation, the related adaline, and the transition to probabilistic generative classification.

The section first completes the discussion of linear discriminant projections by defining projected within- and between-class covariances, an optimization criterion, its eigenvector solution, and the K−1-dimensional rank limitation. It then presents the perceptron as a two-class generalized linear model over fixed nonlinear features, covering its activation, coding, learning criterion, stochastic updates, convergence behavior, historical development, hardware and criticism, and practical limitations. The section concludes by relating the perceptron to adaline and leading toward probabilistic generative classification.

The section develops linear discriminant functions from two-class hyperplane geometry and signed-distance interpretations to multiclass decision rules, highlighting problems with one-versus-one and one-versus-the-rest combinations and presenting unified convex decision regions. It covers least-squares learning for 1-of-K targets, its closed-form solution and limitations, then develops Fisher’s discriminant as a variance-ratio projection method, derives its binary and multiclass forms, establishes its relationship with least squares, and explains thresholding and Gaussian interpretations. It concludes with the perceptron as a nonlinear-feature generalized linear model, including its training, convergence, historical context, limitations, relation to adaline, and connection to probabilistic classification.

nodes.title: 4.2. Probabilistic Generative Models
4.2.1 Continuous inputs
nodes.summary: The text develops probabilistic generative classification using logistic and softmax posteriors. Gaussian class-conditional densities with a shared covariance produce linear logit or softmax scores and linear decision boundaries, with priors shifting boundaries through bias terms; class-specific covariances instead produce quadratic discriminants, while equal-covariance class pairs retain linear boundaries. It then introduces maximum-likelihood estimation of Gaussian parameters and class priors from labeled two-class data, defining binary labels, joint probabilities, the dataset likelihood, and the use of log-likelihood optimization.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Maximum likelihood solution
nodes.summary: The text explains Gaussian generative classification and its maximum likelihood estimation, including priors, class means, and shared covariance, while noting the resulting linear or quadratic decision boundaries and sensitivity to outliers. It then considers discrete features, motivating the naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption to avoid exponentially many parameters, deriving Bernoulli-product class models and linear discriminants, relating the binary case to logistic regression, and beginning the broader exponential-family discussion.

nodes.title: 4.2.3 Discrete features
nodes.summary: The text derives the shared covariance maximum-likelihood estimate for Gaussian class-conditional models as a sample-size-weighted average of the within-class covariances, notes its extension to K classes, and cautions that Gaussian fitting is sensitive to outliers. It then treats binary and general discrete features, explaining the exponential parameter growth of unrestricted distributions and the naive Bayes conditional-independence simplification into Bernoulli factors. This model leads to linear discriminant functions and, for two classes, logistic-sigmoid classification, with analogous results for multistate features. The excerpt concludes by introducing the exponential-family perspective, under which Gaussian and discrete models produce generalized linear posterior class probabilities, and includes several cross-references and exercises.

nodes.title: 4.2.4 Exponential family
nodes.summary: The text completes the shared-covariance Gaussian classification result, noting that the estimated covariance is the sample-size-weighted average of the class covariances, that the result extends to K classes, and that Gaussian fitting is sensitive to outliers. It then develops naive Bayes models for binary and general discrete features, showing that conditional independence avoids exponential parameter growth and produces linear decision functions. More generally, it shows that exponential-family class-conditional distributions with a shared scale lead to logistic or softmax posterior probabilities based on linear functions of the inputs. Finally, it introduces probabilistic discriminative modeling, in which generalized-linear-model parameters are estimated directly by maximum likelihood using iterative reweighted least squares rather than indirectly through class-conditional density estimation.

This section develops generative probabilistic classification from Bayes’ theorem, deriving logistic and softmax posteriors and explaining their log-odds interpretation. Gaussian class-conditional models yield linear boundaries under shared covariance and quadratic boundaries otherwise; their priors, means, and covariances are estimated by maximum likelihood, with noted sensitivity to outliers. For discrete inputs, naive Bayes uses conditional independence to avoid exponential parameter growth and produces linear discriminants equivalent to logistic classification in the two-class case. The section generalizes these results through exponential-family models and concludes by contrasting generative estimation with direct discriminative maximum-likelihood fitting using generalized linear models and iterative reweighted least squares.

nodes.title: 4.3. Probabilistic Discriminative Models
4.3.1 Fixed basis functions
nodes.summary: The text contrasts generative and discriminative classification, then introduces fixed nonlinear basis functions, explaining how they produce nonlinear decision boundaries, handle but cannot remove class overlap, and connect classification to regression while noting their limitations. It next presents two-class logistic regression as a sigmoid applied to a linear feature function, compares its linear parameter growth with the quadratic growth of Gaussian generative models, and begins maximum-likelihood estimation using the sigmoid derivative.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text introduces fixed nonlinear basis-function models, including a bias basis, explaining how they help model overlapping class posteriors while noting that they cannot remove overlap and do not adapt to data. It then develops two-class logistic regression, expressing posterior probabilities through a sigmoid of a linear feature function, and compares its linear parameter growth with the quadratic growth of Gaussian generative models. Maximum likelihood leads to a binary cross-entropy objective whose gradient is the prediction error times the feature vector, enabling sequential updates. Finally, it explains the unbounded-weight overfitting problem for linearly separable data, the resulting nonunique separating solutions, and its resolution through priors/MAP estimation or regularization.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Iterative reweighted least squares
IRLS
nodes.summary: The text derives the logistic-regression Newton update using the parameter-dependent diagonal matrix R, whose entries y_n(1 − y_n) make the Hessian positive definite and ensure a unique error minimum. The update is equivalent to weighted least squares with effective targets z, but must be repeated because the weights depend on w; this yields the IRLS algorithm. The weights are also interpreted as the Bernoulli target variances, and IRLS is explained as solving a locally linearized problem in activation space, with z_n serving as locally adjusted target values.

nodes.title: E[t] var[t]
nodes.summary: The text derives Newton’s method for logistic regression, showing that its parameter-dependent positive-definite Hessian leads to an iterative weighted least-squares algorithm, IRLS. It defines the effective targets and interprets the weights as Bernoulli variances, with IRLS arising from local linearization of the sigmoid. It then introduces multiclass logistic regression using softmax probabilities and linear activations, derives the softmax Jacobian, formulates the 1-of-K likelihood and cross-entropy error, and gives the gradient with respect to each class parameter vector.

The section develops Newton–Raphson optimization for logistic regression, contrasting it with the one-step least-squares solution for quadratic linear-regression error. It derives the logistic cross-entropy gradient and parameter-dependent Hessian, establishes the unique minimum, and reformulates the Newton update as iterative reweighted least squares with variance-based weights and locally adjusted effective targets. It then generalizes the model to multiclass classification through the softmax, deriving its Jacobian, likelihood, cross-entropy objective, and class-specific gradients.

nodes.title: 4.3.4 Multiclass logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text develops multiclass logistic regression as a discriminative model using softmax probabilities generated from linear activations. It derives the softmax derivative, the 1-of-K likelihood, the multiclass cross-entropy error, and its error-times-feature gradient, noting applications to sequential learning and the broader recurrence of this gradient form. It then introduces Newton-Raphson and IRLS batch methods through the block Hessian, states positive definiteness and uniqueness of the error minimum, and references practical implementation details. The text next begins probit regression, motivating alternative binary link functions for cases where generative models do not produce logistic or softmax posteriors and introducing a threshold-based model. It also lists the surrounding section and exercise references.

nodes.title: 4.3.5 Probit regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the multiclass logistic-regression derivation by describing its error-times-feature gradient, Newton-Raphson/IRLS batch method, block Hessian, and unique minimum. It then introduces probit regression through a stochastic threshold model, defining the probit and erf functions, discussing maximum-likelihood estimation, similarity to logistic regression, and greater sensitivity to outliers. It explains how label-flip noise can be incorporated probabilistically. Finally, it begins the general theory of canonical link functions, showing how exponential-family target distributions produce the common error-times-feature gradient structure and relating the conditional mean to the derivative of the log normalizing function.

nodes.title: 4.3.6 Canonical link functions
nodes.summary: The text discusses classifier robustness to outliers and label noise, explaining why probit regression is more outlier-sensitive than logistic regression and giving a probabilistic label-flip model. It then introduces canonical link functions for generalized linear models, derives the exponential-family conditional mean and parameter gradient, and shows that the canonical link reduces the gradient to prediction error times feature vectors. Finally, it begins the discussion of the Laplace approximation as a tool for the intractable Bayesian treatment of logistic regression.

This section develops probabilistic discriminative classification from exponential-family class-conditional models, showing why shared-scale models produce linear logits and softmax activations, and contrasts indirect generative estimation with direct generalized-linear-model maximum likelihood. It introduces fixed nonlinear basis functions and thoroughly derives binary logistic regression, including its likelihood, cross-entropy objective, gradients, sequential learning, parameter efficiency, separability-related overfitting, and MAP or regularization remedies. Newton–Raphson is reformulated as iterative reweighted least squares, then generalized to multiclass softmax regression with its derivatives, likelihood, cross-entropy, block Hessian, and batch optimization. Alternative probit links, threshold-noise modeling, outlier sensitivity, and label noise are discussed, followed by the general canonical-link theory for exponential-family models and an introduction to Laplace approximation for Bayesian logistic regression.

nodes.title: 4.4. The Laplace Approximation
4.4.1 Model comparison and BIC
nodes.summary: The text explains the strengths and limitations of the Laplace approximation, including its dependence on local modes, suitability for large datasets, difficulty with non-real variables, and inability to capture global distributional structure. It then derives its use for approximating Bayesian model evidence, defining the posterior Hessian and the associated Occam complexity penalty, and presents the rough BIC approximation, contrasting it with AIC and noting problems caused by poorly determined parameters. Finally, it introduces Bayesian logistic regression, whose exact posterior and predictive distributions are intractable, and motivates applying the Laplace method with a Gaussian prior and Hessian-based Gaussian approximation around the posterior mode.

The section introduces generalized linear models and the simplifying role of canonical link functions in likelihood gradients, then develops the Laplace approximation by expanding a log density around a local mode and replacing it with a Gaussian determined by the negative curvature or Hessian. It covers the conditions for a valid approximation, numerical mode finding, and an illustrative example; extends the method to multivariate distributions; discusses its practical strengths and limitations; and applies it to Bayesian model evidence, Occam factors, BIC, and Bayesian logistic regression, where it provides a tractable Gaussian approximation to otherwise intractable posterior and predictive calculations.

nodes.title: 4.5. Bayesian Logistic Regression
4.5.1 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains the Laplace approximation to Bayesian model evidence, identifying the Hessian at the posterior mode and the Occam-factor complexity penalty. Under broad-prior and full-rank assumptions this yields the BIC, which penalizes complexity more than AIC, though both criteria may be unreliable when parameters are poorly determined; the full Laplace result is more accurate. It then introduces Bayesian logistic regression, whose exact posterior and predictive inference are intractable, and develops a Laplace solution using a Gaussian prior. The posterior is approximated by a Gaussian centered at the MAP parameter, with covariance given by the inverse Hessian. Predictive class probabilities are obtained by marginalizing the sigmoid over this Gaussian, reducing the integral to the scalar projection a = wTφ and its induced distribution.

nodes.title: 4.5.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops Bayesian logistic regression using a Gaussian prior and a Laplace Gaussian approximation centered at the MAP weight, with covariance determined by the Hessian of the negative log posterior. It derives the predictive class probability by marginalizing the logistic sigmoid over the posterior, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional Gaussian projection with mean wMAP^Tφ and variance φ^TSNφ. Since the resulting sigmoid-Gaussian convolution is intractable, it is approximated through a slope-matched logistic–probit relationship, giving p(C1|φ,t)≈σ(κ(σa^2)μa). The text discusses the unchanged 0.5 decision boundary under equal-cost misclassification and the importance of marginalization for other criteria. It also lists exercises on convex-hull characterizations of linear separability and preservation of linear target constraints by least-squares predictions.

This section introduces Laplace approximation for Bayesian evidence and its Occam-factor penalty, relating it to BIC and contrasting it with AIC. It applies the method to Bayesian logistic regression with a Gaussian prior, approximating the posterior around the MAP estimate using the inverse Hessian. Predictive class probabilities are obtained by reducing sigmoid marginalization to a one-dimensional Gaussian projection and approximating the otherwise intractable sigmoid–Gaussian convolution with a logistic–probit formula. It also discusses decision boundaries and the importance of marginalization for nonstandard criteria, and includes exercises on linear separability and least-squares constraint preservation.

nodes.title: 4.1 ( ) Given a set of data points {x n }, we can define the convex hull to be the set of all points x given by
nodes.summary: The text derives a Gaussian-convolution approximation for the logistic sigmoid and uses it to form an approximate predictive distribution for logistic classification. It explains that posterior marginalization leaves the equal-prior, minimum-error decision boundary unchanged relative to MAP estimation, while potentially affecting other decision criteria, and references a variational-inference illustration. It then presents exercises on the relationship between convex-hull intersection and linear separability, and on preservation of linear constraints from least-squares targets to model predictions.

nodes.title: 4.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text derives a probit-based approximation for integrating a logistic sigmoid over a Gaussian posterior and applies it to logistic predictive probabilities, explaining why marginalization leaves the equal-prior misclassification decision boundary unchanged while affecting more complex decisions. It then presents exercises covering convex-hull characterizations of linear separability, preservation of linear target constraints by least-squares models, Fisher discriminant derivations, logistic-sigmoid identities and inversion, Gaussian generative classification, and maximum-likelihood estimates for multiclass priors and shared-covariance Gaussian means.

nodes.title: 4.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text lists Exercises 4.2–4.10, covering bias terms in linear models, preservation of multiple linear constraints under least squares, derivation of the class-separation and Fisher criteria, least-squares classification using covariance matrices, properties and inversion of the logistic sigmoid, posterior probabilities and parameters for two-class Gaussian generative models, and maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors and Gaussian class means in multiclass generative models.

nodes.title: 4.7 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 4.2–4.10 on linear models, constrained least squares, class separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based formulations, logistic sigmoid properties, Gaussian generative classification, and maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors and class means using 1-of-K targets.

nodes.title: 4.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on linear models for classification, covering bias terms, preservation of linear constraints by least squares, class-separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based least-squares solutions, logistic-sigmoid identities and derivatives, Gaussian generative classifiers, maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors, means, and shared covariance, naive Bayes and softmax linearity, logistic-regression behavior on separable data, Hessian convexity and uniqueness of the optimum, and likelihood formulation for probabilistically mislabeled binary targets.

nodes.title: 4.12 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents maximum-likelihood estimates for class means and a shared covariance in a Gaussian classification model, then lists exercises on naive Bayes and the linearity of softmax arguments for discrete independent features, differentiation of the logistic sigmoid and logistic-regression error, behavior of logistic regression on linearly separable data, positive definiteness of its Hessian and uniqueness of the minimum, and formulation of the likelihood for probabilistically mislabelled binary training data.

nodes.title: 4.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents maximum-likelihood estimates for class means and a shared covariance matrix in Gaussian classification, interpreting the covariance as a class-prior-weighted average. It then lists exercises covering naive Bayes and linear softmax logits, differentiation of the logistic sigmoid and logistic-regression error, behavior of logistic regression on linearly separable data, positive definiteness of its Hessian and uniqueness of the optimum, and likelihood construction for probabilistically labeled binary data.

nodes.title: 4.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 4.17–4.25 cover derivatives and gradients for softmax and cross-entropy functions; gradient and Hessian derivation for probit regression and its use in IRLS; positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian; the relationship between the probit and error functions; derivation of Laplace-approximation model evidence and its reduction to BIC under Gaussian broad priors and i.i.d. data; Gaussian-posterior marginalization in logistic regression; and approximation of the logistic sigmoid by a scaled probit function with λ² = π/8.

nodes.title: 4.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 4.17–4.26 cover derivatives and gradients for softmax and cross-entropy models, gradient and Hessian derivation for probit regression, positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian, the relationship between probit and erf functions, Laplace model evidence and its reduction to BIC under Gaussian broad-prior and i.i.d. assumptions, Gaussian marginalization of logistic regression, matching logistic and scaled-probit sigmoid slopes, and a proof of the Gaussian–probit convolution identity.

This section develops linear models for classification, beginning with class encodings, linear decision geometry, generalized linear models, and the distinction between discriminant, generative, and discriminative approaches. It covers least-squares and Fisher discriminants, perceptrons, and their geometric, statistical, and Gaussian interpretations. It then develops generative classifiers based on Bayes’ theorem, Gaussian and naive-Bayes models, exponential families, logistic and softmax posteriors, and maximum-likelihood estimation. Discriminative treatment focuses on logistic and multiclass softmax regression, optimization by Newton–Raphson and IRLS, regularization, MAP estimation, probit alternatives, noise, separability, and canonical links. Finally, it develops Laplace approximation and applies it to Bayesian evidence and Bayesian logistic regression, including predictive marginalization and sigmoid–Gaussian approximations. The accompanying exercises reinforce derivations and properties of linear models, discriminants, probabilistic classifiers, optimization, Hessians, separability, maximum-likelihood estimates, and Bayesian approximations.

nodes.title: 5 Neural Networks
5.1. Feed-forward Network Functions
5.1.1 Weight-space symmetries
nodes.summary: The text illustrates the expressive power of two-layer neural networks through function approximation and binary classification examples, showing how hidden units combine to form nonlinear mappings and decision boundaries. It then explains weight-space symmetries: sign flips of tanh hidden units and permutations of hidden units yield multiple equivalent parameter vectors, with an overall factor of M!2^M for a two-layer network and multiplicative factors across deeper layers. These symmetries generally have limited practical impact but are relevant to Bayesian model comparison. Finally, it introduces network training as estimating parameters of a nonlinear input-output model, initially through a sum-of-squares error function analogous to polynomial fitting.

This section develops feed-forward neural networks as adaptive nonlinear extensions of linear models. It describes their layered computation from inputs through weighted hidden units to task-specific outputs, including biases, forward propagation, differentiability, and the multilayer perceptron interpretation. It discusses linear-unit limitations, deeper and skip-connected architectures, and conventions for counting layers. It also covers the approximation and classification capabilities of two-layer networks, equivalent parameterizations caused by hidden-unit sign and permutation symmetries, their relevance to Bayesian comparison, and the introduction of network training through sum-of-squares error.

nodes.title: 5.2. Network Training
5.2.1 Parameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text explains the softmax output and its associated multiclass cross-entropy error, including probability constraints, activation-shift degeneracy, regularization, and the correspondence between output/error choices and regression or classification tasks. It then introduces neural-network parameter optimization geometrically, describing gradients, stationary points, minima, maxima, saddle points, equivalent solutions from hidden-unit symmetries, and the distinction between global and local minima. Since analytical optimization is generally infeasible, iterative numerical updates are used, often with gradient evaluations. Finally, it introduces a local quadratic Taylor approximation of the error function as a basis for understanding optimization methods.

nodes.title: 5.2.2 Local quadratic approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains neural-network error minimization, including stationary points, equivalent and inequivalent local minima, and the distinction between global and local minima. Since analytical solutions are unavailable, iterative weight-update methods are used, often with gradient evaluations. It then develops a local quadratic Taylor approximation using the gradient and Hessian, showing that near a minimum the Hessian’s eigenvectors and eigenvalues define elliptical error contours and that positive-definite curvature identifies a minimum. Finally, it explains why gradient information obtained by backpropagation improves optimization and notes that the quadratic error surface contains O(W²) independent information when the network has W adaptive parameters.

nodes.title: 5.2.3 Use of gradient information
nodes.summary: The text explains the quadratic geometry of error functions near stationary points, showing that Hessian eigenvectors define elliptical constant-error contours and that positive Hessian eigenvalues characterize minima. It then motivates gradient-based training through computational complexity, presents batch gradient descent and its learning-rate update, notes its limitations and more efficient alternatives, discusses random restarts and validation, and introduces online or stochastic gradient descent for additive error functions by updating from individual data points.

nodes.title: 5.2.4 Gradient descent optimization
nodes.summary: The text contrasts the high computational cost of derivative-free optimization with the efficiency of gradient-based training, then explains batch gradient descent, its limitations, stronger batch optimizers, repeated random restarts, and online/stochastic and mini-batch alternatives. It describes the efficiency and local-minimum advantages of online updates and introduces error backpropagation as the efficient forward-and-backward computation of network error derivatives, emphasizing that derivative evaluation is distinct from the optimization step and broadly applicable beyond standard multilayer perceptrons and sum-of-squares errors.

This section develops neural-network training from probabilistic modeling and error-function selection to numerical optimization. It derives sum-of-squares regression training from a Gaussian likelihood, explains logistic and softmax outputs with their associated classification cross-entropies, and discusses precision estimation, probability constraints, degeneracies, and regularization. It then examines the nonconvex geometry of parameter space, including stationary points, symmetries, local and global minima, and the Hessian-based quadratic approximation. Finally, it presents gradient-based training methods—batch, stochastic, and mini-batch descent, improved optimizers, random restarts, validation, and backpropagation—emphasizing their computational advantages and practical limitations.

nodes.title: 5.3. Error Backpropagation
5.3.1 Evaluation of error-function derivatives
Error Backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text derives error backpropagation for hidden units using the chain rule, obtaining δj = h′(aj)Σk wkjδk, and explains how recursively propagating output errors backward allows all hidden-unit errors and weight derivatives to be computed. It presents the four-step backpropagation algorithm, describes summing derivatives across patterns for batch training, and notes that different units may use different activation functions. It then introduces a two-layer example with sum-of-squares error, linear outputs, tanh hidden units, the tanh derivative 1 − tanh²(a), and the corresponding forward-propagation equations.

This section develops error backpropagation from a simple linear sum-of-squares model to arbitrary feed-forward networks. It formulates unit activations and forward propagation, applies the chain rule to express each weight derivative as a product of a downstream error signal and an upstream activation, and defines output and recursively propagated hidden-unit errors. It gives the standard backpropagation procedure, explains sequential and batch derivative accumulation and heterogeneous activation functions, and illustrates the formulas with a two-layer linear-output, tanh-hidden network.

nodes.title: 5.3.2 A simple example
nodes.summary: The text explains batch error derivatives, notes that backpropagation extends to units with different activation functions, and works through a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output network with sum-of-squares error. It gives the forward-propagation equations, output and hidden error signals, and gradients for both layers. It then discusses backpropagation's O(W) computational efficiency and contrasts it with forward and central finite-difference derivative estimates, including their respective O(δ) and O(δ^2) errors, extra cost, and loss of O(W) scaling.

nodes.title: 5.3.3 Efficiency of backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text gives the output and hidden error signals and corresponding weight-gradient formulas for a two-layer network, then explains backpropagation’s O(W) efficiency versus the O(W²) cost of forward or central finite differences, including their accuracy and use for software checks. It introduces the Jacobian of network outputs with respect to inputs and explains its role in applying the chain rule and propagating errors through modular differentiable systems.

nodes.title: 5.3.4 The Jacobian matrix
nodes.summary: The text explains how numerical differentiation is used to verify, but not normally replace, efficient backpropagation; develops backpropagation for computing network Jacobians, including their modular chain-rule interpretation, local error propagation, recursive formulas, sigmoid and softmax output cases, computation procedure, and finite-difference validation; and introduces the Hessian of the error with respect to weights and biases, outlining its roles in optimization, retraining, pruning, Bayesian inference, and exact backpropagation-based computation.

This section develops error backpropagation as an efficient chain-rule method for computing gradients in feed-forward neural networks. It distinguishes backward derivative evaluation from subsequent optimization updates, derives output and recursively propagated hidden-unit error signals, and illustrates the method on a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output network with sum-of-squares error. It covers sequential and batch gradient accumulation, varied activations, the O(W) efficiency advantage over finite differences and their accuracy and validation roles, and extends the framework to Jacobian computation for modular networks, including sigmoid and softmax outputs. It also introduces Hessians and their applications in optimization, retraining, pruning, Bayesian inference, and exact computation, while relating gradient evaluation to online, batch, and full-dataset training.

nodes.title: 5.4. The Hessian Matrix
5.4.1 Diagonal approximation
nodes.summary: This section discusses computationally efficient Hessian approximations for neural networks. It presents diagonal approximations, including their recursive evaluation, O(W) cost, an exact-diagonal alternative, and their limitations due to strong off-diagonal structure. It then derives the outer-product or Levenberg–Marquardt approximation for sum-of-squares regression, explains when the neglected residual-dependent term is small, gives its computational cost and validity conditions, and states corresponding forms for logistic cross-entropy and softmax multiclass networks.

nodes.title: 5.4.2 Outer product approximation
nodes.summary: This section derives the Hessian for a neural network using a sum-of-squares regression loss and explains when its residual-dependent second-derivative term can be ignored. This yields the Levenberg–Marquardt or outer-product approximation, which is computationally efficient using backpropagation but is mainly valid near a suitably trained solution. It also gives the corresponding weighted approximation for cross-entropy with sigmoid outputs and notes the analogous softmax result for multiclass networks, along with references to several exercises.

nodes.title: 5.4.3 Inverse Hessian
nodes.summary: The text presents two methods for obtaining or approximating neural-network Hessians. First, an outer-product Hessian approximation is accumulated one data point at a time, and the Woodbury identity provides a recursive update for its inverse, initialized with a small diagonal regularizer and applicable to multiple-output networks. It also notes that quasi-Newton training methods build inverse-Hessian approximations indirectly. Second, mixed second derivatives can be estimated by four-point finite differences, with accuracy constrained by numerical precision and an O(delta^2) approximation error.

nodes.title: 5.4.4 Finite differences
nodes.summary: The text presents methods for approximating and exactly computing neural-network Hessians. An outer-product approximation enables a sequential inverse-Hessian update via the Woodbury identity, initialized with a small diagonal regularizer and extendable to multiple outputs; quasi-Newton methods provide another inverse-Hessian approximation. It then compares direct second-order finite differences, which cost O(W^3), with finite differences of backpropagated gradients, which cost O(W^2), noting their central-difference accuracy and practical use for implementation checks. Finally, it introduces an exact O(W^2) backpropagation-based Hessian method for general differentiable feed-forward networks and begins its two-layer formulation, defining output-error derivatives and giving the Hessian block for pairs of second-layer weights.

nodes.title: 5.4.5 Exact evaluation of the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text compares numerical, exact, and Hessian-vector-product methods for neural-network Hessian computation. Direct symmetric finite differences cost O(W³), while finite differences applied to backpropagated gradients cost O(W²). An exact backpropagation extension computes the Hessian for arbitrary differentiable feed-forward networks in O(W²), with explicit block formulas for a two-layer network and straightforward treatment of biases and skip connections. For applications needing only H multiplied by a vector, Pearlmutter's differential-operator method applies vᵀ∇ to forward- and backpropagation equations to compute the product directly in O(W) time and storage, illustrated for a two-layer linear-output, sum-of-squares network before the excerpt cuts off.

nodes.title: 5.4.6 Fast multiplication by the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text completes formulas for neural-network Hessian elements, including handling biases and skip connections, then develops Pearlmutter’s O(W) method for computing Hessian-vector products by applying R{·} = v^T∇ to standard forward- and backpropagation equations. It derives the required auxiliary forward, backward, and gradient-product equations, explains implementation and recovery of the full Hessian via unit vectors, and introduces regularization as a way to control neural-network complexity. The number of hidden units M affects parameter count and the underfitting–overfitting balance, but validation performance also depends on local minima and initialization; complexity may instead be controlled with a quadratic regularization term.

This section defines the neural-network Hessian and explains its roles in second-order training, rapid retraining, pruning, and Bayesian inference. It develops diagonal, outer-product/Levenberg–Marquardt, and inverse-Hessian approximations; discusses their computational costs, assumptions, and forms for regression, sigmoid cross-entropy, and softmax networks; and presents finite-difference techniques for estimation and verification. It then gives an exact O(W^2) backpropagation method, including treatment of biases and skip connections, and Pearlmutter’s O(W) Hessian-vector-product method. The section concludes by relating regularization and hidden-layer size to model complexity, underfitting, overfitting, initialization, and local-minimum effects.

nodes.title: 5.5. Regularization in Neural Networks
5.5.1 Consistent Gaussian priors
nodes.summary: The text discusses neural-network complexity control through weight decay, consistent Gaussian priors, and early stopping. Standard quadratic weight decay corresponds to a Gaussian weight prior but is not invariant to equivalent rescalings and shifts of network inputs and outputs. A layer-specific penalty excluding biases provides scaling consistency, while grouped Gaussian priors support separate hyperparameters and automatic relevance determination; unconstrained biases make such priors improper unless separately regularized. Figures illustrate network fits, local-minimum effects, and initialization variability. Early stopping instead uses the minimum validation error to prevent overfitting, with effective model complexity increasing throughout training.

nodes.title: 5.5.2 Early stopping
nodes.summary: The text discusses Bayesian interpretations and extensions of neural-network regularization, noting the problems caused by improper weight priors and explaining separate bias priors, grouped weight priors, and automatic relevance determination. It then presents early stopping as an alternative complexity-control method: validation error identifies when to stop, effective model degrees of freedom increase during training, and for quadratic errors early stopping is quantitatively related to weight decay through the iteration-count/learning-rate product. Finally, it introduces input invariances in tasks such as image recognition and speech, explains why learning them solely from transformed examples can be data-intensive, and begins listing four approaches for enforcing them, starting with training-set augmentation.

nodes.title: 5.5.3 Invariances
nodes.summary: The text discusses early stopping as a form of regularization and shows that stopping at the minimum validation error can yield generalization comparable to weight decay. It then introduces invariance requirements in pattern recognition, explains why learning them solely from transformed examples may be impractical, and presents four alternatives: data augmentation, output-invariance regularization, invariant preprocessing features, and invariant network or kernel architectures. Their benefits and limitations are described, including the computational cost of augmentation and possible information loss from hand-crafted features. Finally, tangent propagation is introduced as a regularization method for continuous transformations, representing transformed inputs as manifolds and enforcing locally constant outputs along their tangent directions.

nodes.title: 5.5.4 Tangent propagation
nodes.summary: The text discusses transformation-based regularization in neural networks. It first illustrates synthetic digit warping and notes that hand-crafted invariant features may generalize beyond trained transformations but can lose discriminative information. It then develops tangent propagation: continuous transformations trace manifolds in input space, whose tangent vectors are mapped through the network Jacobian. A regularizer penalizing output variation along these tangents is added to the error, with λ controlling the trade-off between fitting data and enforcing local invariance. Tangents may be estimated by finite differences, derivatives can be obtained through backpropagation, and multiple transformation parameters or transformations are handled by summing regularization terms, yielding local invariance to combinations. Tangent distance provides a related approach for nearest-neighbour methods. Finally, the text introduces augmentation with transformed training data and begins showing its connection to tangent propagation using a single-parameter transformation and sum-of-squares error.

nodes.title: 5.5.5 Training with transformed data
nodes.summary: The text connects tangent distance, tangent propagation, and training on transformed data as methods for encoding invariance. A Taylor expansion shows that augmenting data with small, zero-mean transformations adds a derivative-based regularizer to the original sum-of-squares error; this becomes the tangent-propagation penalty, or Tikhonov regularization for additive noise, with implications for backpropagation and generalization. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as architectural mechanisms for invariance in image recognition, emphasizing local pixel correlations, local feature extraction, and later hierarchical feature combination.

nodes.title: 5.5.6 Convolutional networks
nodes.summary: The text explains how small input-transformation noise produces gradient-based regularization, reducing to Tikhonov regularization for additive noise and relating noise injection to improved generalization. It then introduces convolutional neural networks, which achieve image-transformation invariance through local receptive fields, shared weights, and subsampling, describing feature maps, hierarchical layers, training by constrained backpropagation, and parameter reduction. Finally, it presents soft weight sharing as a learned regularization method that encourages groups of weights to cluster around learned means with learned spreads rather than enforcing exact equality.

nodes.title: 5.5.7 Soft weight sharing
nodes.summary: The text concludes its discussion of convolutional networks by explaining feature maps, local receptive fields, subsampling, progressive shift invariance, fully connected classification outputs, backpropagation with shared weights, and parameter reduction. It then presents soft weight sharing, in which weights are encouraged to form learned groups through a Gaussian-mixture prior. The resulting regularized objective, posterior responsibilities, and derivatives for weights, means, variances, and mixing coefficients are given, including exponential variance and softmax mixing-parameterizations that enforce constraints and prevent degeneracy. Finally, it introduces Mixture Density Networks for modeling multimodal conditional distributions, motivating them with inverse problems such as the two-solution kinematics of a robot arm, disease diagnosis from symptoms, and an incompletely described toy multimodal dataset.

This section presents neural-network regularization as a means of controlling complexity and preventing overfitting. It covers hidden-unit selection, validation-based model comparison, quadratic weight decay and consistent Gaussian priors, bias and grouped-prior issues, automatic relevance determination, and early stopping. It then develops methods for encoding invariances, including data augmentation, invariant features and architectures, tangent propagation, tangent distance, and their connection to noise-induced and Tikhonov regularization. Convolutional networks are described as architectural regularizers using local connectivity, shared weights, feature maps, and subsampling. Finally, soft weight sharing is formulated with Gaussian-mixture priors and constrained parameterizations, followed by an introduction to Mixture Density Networks for multimodal conditional modeling.

nodes.title: 5.6. Mixture Density Networks
nodes.summary: The text introduces mixture density networks as a solution to multimodal inverse problems, using robot-arm kinematics and a toy nonlinear dataset to show why Gaussian least-squares regression can fail. An MDN uses a neural network to predict mixture weights, means, and variances, with softmax and exponential parameterizations enforcing constraints; it is trained by maximum likelihood and optimized through backpropagation using component posterior responsibilities. The resulting conditional density can represent changing unimodal or multimodal behavior and supports computation of conditional means, input-dependent variances, and approximate modes, with ordinary least-squares regression as a special case. The text then begins Bayesian neural networks, contrasting maximum-likelihood or MAP estimation with Bayesian parameter marginalization and noting that nonlinear, nonconvex neural-network posteriors require approximate methods such as factorized-Gaussian variational inference.

nodes.title: 5.7. Bayesian Neural Networks
5.7.1 Posterior parameter distribution
nodes.summary: This section develops Bayesian neural-network regression using a Laplace approximation to the weight posterior and a local linearization of the network around its MAP weights. It specifies Gaussian likelihood and weight-prior models, derives the regularized posterior and its Hessian-based Gaussian approximation, and obtains a Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty. It then applies the evidence framework to estimate α and β and compare network architectures, deriving the approximate log evidence and introducing Hessian eigenvalues and the effective parameter count for hyperparameter updates. Classification extensions are deferred to a later discussion.

nodes.title: 5.7.2 Hyperparameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text describes Bayesian neural-network regression predictions, whose Gaussian mean is the MAP network output and whose variance combines intrinsic noise with input-dependent parameter uncertainty. It then explains evidence-based optimization of alpha and beta using a Laplace approximation, giving the approximate log evidence, regularized error, Hessian-eigenvalue effective parameter count, and alternating re-estimation formulas. It discusses complications from neural-network multimodal posteriors, initialization dependence, equivalent and inequivalent solutions, evidence-based model comparison, difficulties evaluating Hessian determinants, and correction for hidden-unit permutation and sign symmetries. Finally, it introduces the forthcoming treatment of Bayesian neural networks for classification.

nodes.title: 5.7.3 Bayesian neural networks for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the evidence-based Laplace treatment of Bayesian neural-network regression, giving effective-parameter and β re-estimation formulas, discussing alternating hyperparameter optimization, multimodal posteriors, symmetry-equivalent solutions, model evidence, and practical Hessian-determinant issues. It then develops Bayesian neural-network classification with a logistic output: cross-entropy likelihood, Gaussian prior and MAP regularization, Hessian-based Laplace posterior, evidence optimization for α, and approximate predictive probabilities obtained by linearizing the output activation and integrating over weight uncertainty. Examples illustrate reduced overfitting and less confident predictions after marginalization. The excerpt concludes with exercises on sigmoid–tanh network equivalence and the equivalence between multioutput likelihood maximization and sum-of-squares minimization.

The section transitions from mixture density networks, emphasizing their input-dependent uncertainty and usefulness for multimodal predictions, to Bayesian neural networks. It explains why exact inference is infeasible in multilayer networks, develops Laplace-approximated posterior and predictive distributions for regression, and uses evidence and Hessian-based effective parameter counts to optimize hyperparameters and compare models while addressing multimodality and network symmetries. It then extends the approach to logistic classification through cross-entropy likelihoods, Gaussian priors, MAP estimation, Laplace uncertainty, and approximate predictive probabilities, illustrating reduced overfitting and confidence, and concludes with related exercises.

nodes.title: 5.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of Laplace approximations for Bayesian neural networks, explaining an analytically intractable sigmoid-Gaussian convolution and an approximation for the posterior predictive probability. It uses Figure 5.23 to show that Bayesian marginalization makes predictions less confident while preserving the decision boundary. This chapter presents multilayer perceptrons as compact adaptive nonlinear models for statistical pattern recognition, covering their architectures, approximation properties, parameter symmetries, probabilistic objectives, and practical training. It develops gradient computation through backpropagation and Hessian-based methods, including efficient Jacobian and Hessian-vector calculations, and examines nonconvex optimization, initialization, validation, and model-complexity effects. It then surveys regularization through weight penalties, priors, early stopping, invariance methods, convolutional and shared-weight architectures, and soft weight sharing. Mixture density networks are introduced for multimodal conditional prediction, followed by Bayesian neural networks using approximate posterior and predictive inference, evidence-based comparison, and uncertainty estimation. Exercises reinforce the chapter’s derivations and applications involving likelihoods, derivatives, optimization, Hessians, regularization, mixture models, kinematics, and Bayesian prediction.

nodes.title: 6 Kernel Methods
6.1. Dual Representations
nodes.summary: The text derives the dual form of regularized linear least-squares regression. Setting the gradient with respect to w to zero expresses w as a combination of training feature vectors, allowing the objective to be reformulated in terms of coefficients a and the Gram matrix K of feature-vector inner products. Solving gives a = (K + λ I)^{-1}t, and predictions are kernel-weighted combinations of training targets. The dual form may be computationally less efficient when N exceeds the feature dimension M, but its key benefit is that it uses only kernel evaluations, implicitly supporting very high- or infinite-dimensional feature spaces. The text also notes applications to other models and introduces kernel construction: kernels may be obtained from feature mappings or defined directly, provided they represent valid inner products; the squared inner-product kernel is given as an example.

nodes.title: 6.2. Constructing Kernels
nodes.summary: The text derives the dual kernel formulation of regularized linear regression, showing that predictions are weighted combinations of training targets based only on kernel evaluations and explaining its computational tradeoff and usefulness for implicit high- or infinite-dimensional feature spaces. It then explains how kernels arise from feature mappings, how validity is tested through positive-semidefinite Gram matrices, and how new kernels can be constructed from existing ones. Examples include polynomial, Gaussian, generalized distance, set, generative-model, hidden-Markov-model, Fisher, and sigmoidal kernels, with discussion of their properties and limitations. Finally, it introduces radial basis function networks, covering their distance-based basis functions, exact interpolation use, overfitting with noisy targets, and their connection to regularization and Green's functions.

nodes.title: 6.3. Radial Basis Function Networks
6.3.1 Nadaraya-Watson model
nodes.summary: The text discusses selecting centres for radial basis functions and introduces the Nadaraya-Watson kernel-regression model. Starting from Parzen estimation of the joint input-target density, it derives a normalized kernel-weighted average of training targets, explains its locality and summation constraint, and gives the associated full conditional distribution. Gaussian components produce a Gaussian-mixture conditional model illustrated for sinusoidal data, while more flexible components and joint Gaussian mixture models offer extensions and possible faster prediction. The section concludes by transitioning to Gaussian processes.

This section introduces radial basis function networks as linear models whose basis functions depend on distance from centres. It covers their origins in exact interpolation, their appearance as regularized Green’s-function expansions, and their derivation under noisy inputs, including normalized bases and the Nadaraya-Watson model. It explains why normalization is useful, describes reducing computational cost by using fewer data-selected centres fitted by least squares, and develops the Nadaraya-Watson model from Parzen density estimation as normalized kernel regression with a conditional distribution. Gaussian kernels lead to Gaussian-mixture conditionals, with more flexible and joint-mixture extensions, and the section closes by relating these models to Gaussian processes.

nodes.title: 6.4. Gaussian Processes
6.4.1 Linear regression revisited
nodes.summary: The text introduces Gaussian processes as Bayesian distributions over functions and motivates them through Bayesian linear regression. A Gaussian prior over linear-model weights induces a Gaussian distribution over function values, whose covariance is a kernel Gram matrix; this leads to the general definition of a Gaussian process, specified by its mean and covariance kernel. It discusses zero-mean processes, Gaussian and exponential kernels, related models such as kriging and Kalman filters, and then formulates Gaussian-process regression with independent Gaussian observation noise, deriving the latent-value and marginal target distributions and explaining how kernels represent input similarity.

nodes.title: 6.4.2 Gaussian processes for regression
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian process regression with independent Gaussian observation noise, deriving the Gaussian marginal distribution of observed targets and the kernel-based predictive mean and variance obtained by conditioning a joint Gaussian. It presents a standard quadratic-exponential kernel with constant and linear components, discusses kernel validity, radial-basis expansions, the equivalence with finite-basis Bayesian linear regression, computational costs and large-data approximations, and extensions such as co-kriging, manifold learning, and stochastic differential equations. It then explains learning covariance hyperparameters through marginal-likelihood or posterior optimization, gives the likelihood and its gradient, notes nonconvexity and the difficulty of full Bayesian marginalization, and introduces the motivation for input-dependent noise in heteroscedastic models. Figures illustrate kernel and Gaussian-process samples, noisy observations, conditioning, and regression uncertainty.

nodes.title: 6.4.3 Learning the hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text discusses learning Gaussian process hyperparameters, including covariance length scales and noise precision, by likelihood maximization with gradient-based optimization, gives the log likelihood and its gradient, and notes nonconvexity, priors, and the need for approximations in fully Bayesian inference. It extends Gaussian processes to heteroscedastic noise by modeling input-dependent log precision with a second process. It then introduces automatic relevance determination, whose input-specific kernel parameters reveal and potentially remove irrelevant variables, illustrating the effect with prior samples and the beginning of a synthetic three-input example.

nodes.title: 6.4.4 Automatic relevance determination
nodes.summary: The text introduces heteroscedastic Gaussian processes that model the logarithm of an input-dependent variance, then develops automatic relevance determination (ARD), which uses separate kernel precision parameters for each input and learns their relevance by marginal-likelihood optimization. It explains the ARD kernel, shows how small precisions indicate insensitivity and possible feature removal, and describes figures illustrating this effect. A three-input synthetic example demonstrates that ARD assigns the largest precision to the strongest predictor, a smaller one to a noisy correlated predictor, and a near-zero value to an irrelevant predictor. The ARD extension of the exponential-quadratic kernel is given explicitly. Finally, the text begins Gaussian-process classification, explaining the use of a logistic sigmoid on a latent Gaussian process to obtain valid binary-class probabilities in (0, 1).

nodes.title: 6.4.5 Gaussian processes for classification
nodes.summary: The text first explains ARD in Gaussian processes through a synthetic three-input example and gives the resulting input-dependent kernel. It then introduces Gaussian-process classification: latent Gaussian-process functions are passed through a logistic sigmoid to model Bernoulli targets, with a covariance matrix augmented by a small numerical term. The binary predictive probability is an intractable integral over the latent posterior. Sampling and several Gaussian approximations are discussed, including variational inference, expectation propagation, and the Laplace approximation; variational methods can extend to multiclass problems. The text then begins the detailed Laplace treatment by deriving the test-point latent posterior via Bayes’ theorem and marginalization.

nodes.title: 6.4.6 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text presents Gaussian-process classification, focusing on approximating the intractable logistic predictive integral through Gaussian approximations. It reviews variational inference and expectation propagation, then develops the Laplace approximation in detail: deriving the latent posterior, its mode via Newton–Raphson/IRLS, the Hessian and Gaussian posterior approximation, predictive mean and variance, and approximate class probabilities. It also derives the Laplace marginal likelihood and its covariance-parameter gradients, illustrates classification on synthetic data, notes extension to multiclass softmax models, and explains the infinite-width connection between Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, including the loss of output coupling and the nonstationary kernels induced by probit or Gaussian activations.

nodes.title: 6.4.7 Connection to neural networks
nodes.summary: The text presents an illustration of Gaussian-process classification, explains the connection between infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes—including the loss of output coupling, nonstationary kernels, and hyperparameter treatment—and concludes with exercises on dual formulations, perceptron and nearest-neighbour kernelization, positive-definite matrices, valid-kernel constructions, and a kernel tailored to a target function.

It then develops Gaussian-process classification with logistic latent functions, covering intractable prediction and approximation methods, especially the Laplace approximation and its optimization, predictive, and marginal-likelihood calculations. The section concludes with multiclass considerations, the connection between infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, illustrative examples, and exercises on kernel methods and positive-definite constructions.

This section develops kernel methods from memory-based prediction and dual representations to kernel construction, radial basis networks, and Gaussian processes. It defines kernels as feature-space inner products and explains the kernel trick, valid positive-semidefinite constructions, common kernel families, and computational implications. nodes.title: 7 Sparse Kernel Machines
7.1. Maximum Margin Classifiers
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
nodes.summary: The text derives the kernelized dual formulation of the maximum-margin classifier, explains its constraints, computational implications, and the importance of positive-definite kernels, and gives the kernel-based prediction rule. It uses the KKT conditions to identify support vectors, explains how to compute the bias term, and reformulates the classifier with an infinite-penalty error function and quadratic regularization. A Gaussian-kernel example demonstrates nonlinear separation and sparsity. The section then introduces overlapping class distributions and slack variables to allow margin violations with linear penalties, and includes a biographical note on Joseph-Louis Lagrange.

nodes.title: 7.1.1 Overlapping class distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains Gaussian-kernel SVM geometry and sparsity, then develops the soft-margin SVM for overlapping classes using slack variables, its objective, KKT conditions, dual formulation, support-vector interpretation, and bias estimation. It introduces ν-SVM and interprets ν, discusses kernel quadratic-programming training methods including chunking, decomposition, and SMO, explains why kernels do not avoid effective dimensionality limitations, and describes Platt sigmoid calibration for probabilistic outputs and its limitations. It concludes by beginning a comparison between nonseparable SVMs and regularized logistic regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.2 Relation to logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text explains dependencies in polynomial-kernel feature mappings, showing that a nominally six-dimensional feature representation of two-dimensional inputs lies on a constrained nonlinear manifold. It then discusses converting SVM decisions into probabilities through Platt’s sigmoid calibration and the limitations of this two-stage approach. Nonseparable SVMs are reformulated as regularized hinge-loss minimization and compared with regularized logistic regression and squared-error classification losses, emphasizing hinge-loss sparsity and the drawbacks of squared error. Finally, it surveys multiclass SVM strategies, including one-versus-the-rest, modified target coding, and joint Weston-Watkins optimization, along with their consistency, calibration, class-balance, and computational-cost issues.

nodes.title: 7.1.3 Multiclass SVMs
nodes.summary: The text compares classification error functions, explaining that the flat region of hinge/support-vector loss yields sparse solutions, while logistic and hinge losses approximate misclassification error and squared error can overemphasize confidently correct points. It surveys multiclass SVM strategies—one-versus-the-rest, target-adjusted variants, joint optimization, one-versus-one voting, DAGSVM, and error-correcting output codes—discussing their ambiguities, class imbalance, robustness, and computational costs, and notes that one-versus-the-rest is most common. It also describes one-class SVMs for enclosing a chosen high-density region using either a separating hyperplane or a minimum enclosing sphere, with equivalence for translation-invariant kernels, before introducing sparse SVM regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.4 SVMs for regression
nodes.summary: The text discusses multiclass and single-class SVMs, SVM regression, and the foundations of computational learning theory. It compares one-versus-one, DAGSVM, error-correcting output codes, and the commonly used one-versus-the-rest strategy; explains single-class SVMs as high-density region estimators; and develops ε-insensitive support vector regression, including its slack-variable formulation, Lagrangian and dual optimization, kernel prediction equation, box and KKT constraints, sparse support-vector interpretation, bias estimation, and the ν-SVM alternative with bounds on outliers and support vectors. A sinusoidal Gaussian-kernel example is noted, with parameters typically selected by cross-validation. The section concludes by defining PAC generalization, its probability and error requirements, training-size goals, and the role of VC dimension in measuring model complexity.

nodes.title: 7.1.5 Computational learning theory
nodes.summary: The text concludes the SVM discussion with an illustration of ν-SVM regression, then reviews computational learning theory and PAC learning, including its error criterion, probability guarantee, sample-size goal, VC dimension, worst-case conservatism, and the PAC-Bayesian refinement. It next introduces Relevance Vector Machines as Bayesian sparse-kernel alternatives to SVMs that provide probabilistic outputs, address multiclass and parameter-selection issues, use sparser models, and retain comparable generalization. The RVM treatment begins with regression, modeled as a linear model with a sparsity-inducing prior and Gaussian conditional target distribution.

This section develops support vector machines from maximum-margin linear classification through kernelization, dual optimization, KKT-based support-vector sparsity, bias estimation, and nonlinear Gaussian-kernel examples. It extends SVMs to overlapping classes with soft margins and ν-SVMs, relates them to hinge-loss regularization and logistic or squared-error classification, and discusses training algorithms, kernel dimensionality, and probabilistic calibration. It covers multiclass and one-class SVM strategies, ε-insensitive and ν-SVM regression, and concludes with PAC and VC-dimension foundations of computational learning theory before introducing Bayesian relevance vector machines as typically sparser, probabilistic alternatives. A biographical note on Lagrange is also included.

nodes.title: 7.2. Relevance Vector Machines
7.2.1 RVM for regression
nodes.summary: The text first explains why standard and PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are usually too conservative. It then introduces the relevance vector machine as a Bayesian sparse-kernel alternative to SVMs, describing its Gaussian regression model, independent weight-precision priors, evidence-based hyperparameter learning, Gaussian posterior and predictive distributions, automatic relevance determination, and the resulting relevance vectors. RVMs provide probabilistic predictions, flexible basis functions, and typically much sparser models than SVMs with similar accuracy, though they can suffer from poor extrapolation uncertainty, nonconvex and potentially slower training, and cubic matrix-inversion costs. A regression example illustrates the sparsity advantage, and the text concludes by beginning a more detailed analysis of the sparsity mechanism.

nodes.title: 7.2.2 Analysis of sparsity
Sequential Sparse Bayesian Learning Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how the quality and sparsity measures determine marginal-likelihood maxima for each RVM hyperparameter: q_i^2 > s_i yields a finite closed-form α_i update, while q_i^2 ≤ s_i leads to α_i = ∞ and pruning. It presents the resulting sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm for adding, updating, and removing basis functions, gives efficient formulas for q_i and s_i through Q_i and S_i, and notes the O(M^3) cost based on active vectors. It then introduces the RVM extension to binary classification using an ARD prior and a logistic-sigmoid linear model.

This section explains why relevance vector machines are highly sparse: automatic relevance determination prunes basis functions that are poorly aligned with the data by sending their precision parameters to infinity. It develops both geometric intuition and a marginal-likelihood analysis based on per-basis sparsity and quality measures, then uses their explicit stationary conditions to formulate a sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm for adding, updating, and removing relevance vectors efficiently. It also contrasts RVM compactness, computational costs, and automatic hyperparameter selection with SVMs, and introduces the RVM extension to binary logistic classification.

It then develops RVM classification: binary logistic classification with an ARD prior is treated using IRLS and a Laplace posterior approximation, yielding posterior formulas, marginal likelihood, hyperparameter updates, and the same sparsity algorithm as regression. The RVM is extended to multiclass softmax models, providing probabilistic predictions and a principled alternative to pairwise SVM classification at higher computational cost. RVM relevance vectors, sparsity, training and prediction costs are compared with SVMs. The section concludes with exercises on Parzen and feature-space nearest-mean classification, maximum-margin hyperplanes and dual variables, logistic regression regularization, and deriving the regression SVM dual.

It covers binary logistic RVMs with IRLS and Laplace inference, multiclass softmax extensions, computational and predictive trade-offs against SVMs, illustrative regression results, and exercises on related classification, margin, logistic-regression, and SVM-duality topics.
