This section surveys sparse kernel methods, beginning with the computational motivation and convex optimization framework of support vector machines. It develops maximum-margin, kernelized, soft-margin, ν-, multiclass, one-class, classification, regression, and probabilistically calibrated SVMs, together with learning-theory foundations and a note on Lagrange. It then presents Bayesian ARD-based relevance vector machines for regression and classification, covering their probabilistic inference, evidence optimization, sparsity, sequential selection, predictive behavior, multiclass extensions, and computational comparison with SVMs. The accompanying exercises derive and verify core SVM, logistic-regression, and RVM results, including duality, support-vector conditions, posterior and predictive distributions, marginal likelihoods, hyperparameter updates, sparsity measures, matrix identities, and classification-RVM derivatives.

nodes.title: 8 Graphical Models
8.1. Bayesian Networks
8.1.1 Example: Polynomial regression
nodes.summary: The text explains how directed acyclic graphs encode joint distributions through products of node conditionals given their parents, using a seven-variable example and emphasizing normalization and acyclicity. It applies this framework to Bayesian polynomial regression, introducing plates for repeated observations, explicit deterministic parameters, graphical notation for observed and latent variables, posterior inference for coefficients, and predictive inference for new inputs by integrating over coefficients. It concludes with generative modeling through ancestral sampling, in which variables are sampled in parent-to-child order to obtain joint or marginal samples.

nodes.title: 8.1.2 Generative models
nodes.summary: The text explains how Bayesian predictive distributions are formed by integrating out model parameters, then introduces ancestral sampling for directed graphical models and shows how to obtain joint or marginal samples by sequentially sampling nodes in parent-to-child order. It describes generative models, where latent variables and conditional distributions represent the causal creation of observations, illustrated by object images governed by identity, position, and orientation. It contrasts these with nongenerative polynomial regression, discusses the possible physical or abstract roles of latent variables, and explains that synthetic samples from generative models can illuminate their implied data distributions. The section concludes by introducing discrete variables and the role of exponential-family distributions as components of complex models.

nodes.title: 8.1.3 Discrete variables
nodes.summary: The text explains how graphical models represent latent variables and observed data, especially in generative object-recognition models where object identity, position, and orientation generate an image. It contrasts generative models with polynomial regression, discusses the role of latent variables and ancestral sampling, and introduces discrete Bayesian networks. It derives parameter counts for multinomial variables, general joint distributions, independent variables, chains, and tied parameters, showing how graph sparsity and parameter sharing control exponential growth. It also describes adding Dirichlet priors and replacing exponentially large conditional-probability tables with logistic-sigmoid parameterizations that use linearly many parameters while imposing modeling restrictions.

nodes.title: 8.1.4 Linear-Gaussian models
nodes.summary: The text develops linear-Gaussian graphical models, showing how Gaussian conditional distributions in a directed acyclic graph combine into a multivariate Gaussian joint distribution. It derives recursive formulas for means and covariances, examines independent, fully connected, and partially connected graphs, and explains their parameterization and covariance constraints. The model is generalized to multivariate nodes and connected to conjugate priors, hyperpriors, and hierarchical Bayesian modeling. The text then introduces conditional independence and its equivalent factorization of a conditional joint distribution.

This section introduces Bayesian networks within the broader framework of graphical models, explaining how directed acyclic graphs encode joint distributions through products of conditional distributions and how graph structure expresses independence, causality, and computational organization. It develops examples involving polynomial regression and generative modeling, including plates, latent and observed variables, posterior and predictive inference, and ancestral sampling. It then treats discrete networks, analyzing parameter growth, sparsity, parameter sharing, Dirichlet priors, and logistic-sigmoid parameterizations, before developing linear-Gaussian networks, their mean and covariance structure, multivariate and hierarchical extensions, conjugate priors, and conditional independence.

nodes.title: 8.2. Conditional Independence
8.2.1 Three example graphs
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional independence and the d-separation method for reading such relationships directly from directed acyclic graphs. Through three-node tail-to-tail, head-to-tail, and head-to-head examples, it shows that conditioning blocks ordinary paths but opens collider paths, especially when a collider or its descendant is observed. A battery, fuel-tank, and unreliable fuel-gauge example demonstrates explaining away numerically. The section concludes with the general d-separation rule: all paths between two node sets must be blocked by conditioned noncolliders or unobserved colliders for the corresponding conditional independence to be implied.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 D-separation
nodes.summary: The text illustrates explaining away with a fuel-tank, gauge, and battery example, then defines d-separation for directed graphs, including its path-blocking rules, examples, treatment of parameter nodes, and implications for conditional independence. It applies these ideas to i.i.d. Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, and the naive Bayes classifier, explaining conditional versus marginal dependence, modeling benefits, and limitations. It presents the d-separation theorem as equivalent to directed factorization, discusses the range of distributions represented by different graph structures, and defines the Markov blanket as a node’s parents, children, and co-parents. Finally, it introduces Markov random fields as undirected graphical models that specify factorizations and independences through ordinary graph separation.

This section extends graphical models to multivariate linear-Gaussian variables and hierarchical Bayesian constructions, then defines conditional independence through conditional distributions and factorization. It develops d-separation for directed graphs using three-node structures and the explaining-away example, explaining how conditioning blocks or opens paths and how graph structure implies independence. The ideas are applied to Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, and naive Bayes, followed by the d-separation theorem, discussion of representable distributions and Markov blankets, and an introduction to undirected Markov random fields and their separation-based independences.

nodes.title: 8.3. Markov Random Fields
8.3.1 Conditional independence properties
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of directed-graph Markov blankets and introduces Markov random fields. It explains that a directed node is isolated by its parents, children, and children’s other parents, since explaining away creates dependencies with co-parents. Markov random fields use undirected graphs to represent variables and links, specifying both factorizations and conditional independences. Their conditional-independence criterion is ordinary graph separation: A is independent of B given C when removing C disconnects A from B, with no explaining-away complication. The Markov blanket in this setting is simply a node’s neighbors. The section then begins developing the corresponding undirected factorization in terms of functions over local variable sets.

nodes.title: 8.3.2 Factorization properties
nodes.summary: The text explains conditional independence and factorization in undirected graphical models. Independence is determined by graph separation: all paths between two node sets must pass through the conditioning set, or equivalently no connecting path remains after removing that set. Undirected graphs avoid directed-graph issues such as parent-child asymmetry and explaining away, and their Markov blankets consist simply of neighboring nodes. The joint distribution factors into nonnegative potential functions over maximal cliques, with an explicit partition-function normalization that may be computationally expensive but is unnecessary for certain local conditional or marginal calculations. For strictly positive potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem establishes equivalence between graph-separation independences and clique factorization. Potentials may be represented exponentially through energy functions, with global probabilities reflecting the balance of local clique preferences. The section concludes by introducing binary image denoising, modeling noisy and clean pixels as ±1 variables with pixel-flip noise and exploiting correlations between corresponding and neighboring pixels.

nodes.title: 8.3.3 Illustration: Image de-noising
nodes.summary: The text explains the equivalence, for strictly positive distributions, between conditional independencies represented by separation in an undirected graph and factorization over maximal cliques via the Hammersley–Clifford theorem. It introduces Boltzmann potentials and energy functions, emphasizing that undirected potentials express preferences among configurations rather than conditional probabilities. It then develops a binary-image de-noising Markov random field with data-agreement, neighboring-pixel, and optional bias energies, derives its joint distribution and conditional restoration problem, and describes ICM optimization, its local-maxima limitation, and improved max-product and globally optimal graph-cut methods for suitable models. Finally, it begins relating undirected models to directed graphs by converting a directed chain factorization into an undirected pairwise-clique factorization.

nodes.title: 8.3.4 Relation to directed graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes discussion of image denoising optimization and then explains how directed graphical models relate to undirected Markov random fields. Directed factorizations can be converted through moralization—connecting co-parents, removing directions, and assigning conditional factors to clique potentials—with Z = 1; this is useful for exact inference but may lose independencies. It defines D maps, I maps, and perfect maps, shows that directed and undirected graphs represent different conditional-independence patterns, and introduces chain graphs as a broader but still non-universal framework. Finally, it begins the topic of graphical-model inference, involving posterior computation with observed nodes while exploiting graph structure for efficiency.

This section introduces Markov random fields as undirected graphical models whose conditional independencies are determined by graph separation and whose distributions factor over maximal cliques, with neighboring nodes forming each variable’s Markov blanket. It develops clique potentials, partition functions, the Hammersley–Clifford equivalence for positive distributions, and energy-based interpretations. A binary image-denoising example models data agreement, pixel correlations, and bias, deriving restoration objectives and comparing ICM, max-product, and graph-cut optimization. The section then relates undirected and directed models through moralization, discusses D maps, I maps, perfect maps, and chain graphs, and begins the topic of efficient inference with observed variables.

nodes.title: 8.4. Inference in Graphical Models
8.4.1 Inference on a chain
nodes.summary: The text introduces exact inference in graphical models through Bayes’ theorem and then develops sum-product message passing on an undirected chain. Direct marginalization of the full joint distribution is exponential, but exploiting conditional independence and distributivity yields forward and backward messages whose pointwise product gives each node marginal in O(NK^2) time. Messages can be reused to compute all node and neighboring-node or clique marginals efficiently, observations are handled by clamping variables with indicator functions, and the resulting local distributions support EM parameter learning. The chain algorithm is also related to Chapman–Kolmogorov equations for Markov chains, and inference on trees is announced as the next topic.

nodes.title: 8.4.2 Trees
nodes.summary: The text explains how bidirectional message passing efficiently computes every marginal in a chain, including handling observed variables through indicator-function clamping and obtaining neighboring-variable joint distributions from stored messages. These local clique distributions support EM parameter learning with missing data. It then generalizes exact inference from chains to trees via the sum-product algorithm, defining undirected trees, directed rooted trees, and polytrees and describing their relationships through moralization. Finally, it introduces factor graphs as an explicit, unified representation of joint distributions factored into functions over variable subsets.

nodes.title: 8.4.3 Factor graphs
nodes.summary: The text introduces tree-structured graphs as the setting for efficient local message-passing inference, defining undirected trees, directed trees, and directed polytrees and explaining their relationships through moralization. It then develops factor graphs, bipartite representations that explicitly separate variables from factors and can encode directed conditional distributions or undirected clique potentials, often in multiple equivalent forms. Examples show how factors may be combined or kept separate, how tree and polytree structures transform, and how factor graphs preserve detailed factorizations without necessarily encoding additional conditional independencies. Finally, it introduces the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference on tree-structured factor graphs, with sums for discrete variables and integrals for continuous models, and previews the max-sum algorithm for finding the most probable state.

nodes.title: 8.4.4 The sum-product algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how factor graphs represent directed and undirected graphical models while retaining tree structure, then derives the sum-product message-passing algorithm for exact marginal inference on such graphs. It defines factor-to-variable and variable-to-factor messages, leaf initialization, recursive propagation, efficient computation of all variable and factor marginals, normalization for unnormalized undirected models, and an illustrative four-variable example. It also describes conditioning on observed variables through indicator functions and extending the method from discrete sums to continuous integrals. Finally, it introduces max-sum as a dynamic-programming method for finding the globally most probable variable assignment, emphasizing that separate marginal maxima need not form the joint maximum.

nodes.title: 8.4.5 The max-sum algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces max-sum inference as the dynamic-programming counterpart of sum-product for finding both the maximum joint probability and a corresponding variable assignment. It demonstrates why marginal maximization is insufficient, derives max-product and its log-domain max-sum form using distributive identities, and gives the associated leaf-to-root message updates. Because ties can make independent node decisions inconsistent, it explains storing maximizing predecessor assignments and using backtracking, first for chains and then for arbitrary tree factor graphs. The method is exact on trees, underlies the Viterbi algorithm, accommodates observed variables by clamping, and is contrasted with the simpler but non-global ICM algorithm.

nodes.title: 8.4.6 Exact inference in general graphs
nodes.summary: The text explains exact inference in loopy graphical models through the junction tree algorithm: moralization, triangulation, clique-based maximum spanning-tree construction, the running intersection property, and junction-tree message passing for exact marginals and conditionals. It discusses computational complexity through clique size and treewidth. It then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate application of local sum-product updates to cyclic graphs, covering convergence uncertainty, unit-message initialization, flooding and serial schedules, and the definition and handling of pending messages.

nodes.title: 8.4.7 Loopy belief propagation
nodes.summary: The text explains how junction-tree complexity is characterized by minimized treewidth and why high treewidth limits exact inference. It then presents loopy belief propagation as an approximate sum-product method for graphs with cycles, covering initialization, message updates, pending messages, scheduling, termination or convergence, marginal estimation, and applications to error-correcting-code decoding. Finally, it introduces Bayesian learning of graph structure, including posterior scoring by model evidence, computational difficulties from latent-variable marginalization and the exponential search space, and states two exercises on normalization of directed-graph factorizations and the relationship between node orderings and acyclicity.

nodes.title: 8.4.8 Learning the graph structure
nodes.summary: The text explains termination and accuracy properties of belief propagation on trees versus loopy graphs, including its practical convergence and applications to error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graphical-model structure, using posterior structure probabilities and model evidence while noting the computational difficulty of latent-variable marginalization and exponentially large structure spaces. Two exercises concern normalization of directed-graph factorizations and the relationship between node orderings and absence of directed cycles.

This section introduces inference in graphical models, beginning with the representational limits of directed, undirected, and chain graphs. It develops exact message-passing inference on chains and trees, including sum-product computation of marginals, handling of observations, continuous variables, clique distributions, and EM learning, then presents factor graphs as a unified factorized representation. It derives sum-product and max-sum algorithms, including dynamic programming, backtracking, MAP assignment, and the Viterbi connection. For general graphs it explains exact junction-tree inference and its treewidth-based complexity, followed by approximate loopy belief propagation, its scheduling and convergence issues, and applications such as code decoding. The section concludes with Bayesian learning of graph structure, model evidence, computational difficulties, and related exercises.

It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structure from data, including posterior structure scoring, model evidence, and the computational difficulties caused by latent-variable marginalization and exponentially many candidate graphs. It concludes with exercises on normalization of directed-graph joint distributions and the relationship between node ordering and the absence of directed cycles.

nodes.title: 8.2 ( ) www

It then introduces Bayesian learning of graphical-model structure, where candidate graphs are scored through posterior probability and model evidence, noting the computational difficulty of latent-variable marginalization and exponential structure search. The exercises cover normalization and acyclicity of directed graphical models, dependence and conditional independence using an explicitly tabulated three-variable distribution, factorization and graph construction, a relevance-vector-machine graph, the noisy-OR model, recursive Gaussian moments, independence implications, and Markov-blanket d-separation.

nodes.title: 8.5 ( ) www

They cover verifying marginal and conditional independence from a tabulated binary joint distribution, deriving probability factorizations and graphs, constructing a graphical model for a relevance vector machine, interpreting the noisy-OR model and its leak parameter, deriving Gaussian means and covariances via recursion, proving an implication between conditional-independence statements, and establishing the Markov-blanket conditional-independence property using d-separation.

nodes.summary: The text presents a joint distribution for three binary variables and exercises on verifying marginal and conditional independence, deriving probability factorizations and their directed graphs, representing a relevance vector machine graphically, interpreting the noisy-OR model as a soft logical OR, deriving Gaussian moments through recursion, proving a conditional-independence decomposition, and establishing the Markov-blanket conditional-independence property using d-separation.

nodes.title: 8.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents graphical-model exercises covering joint and conditional independence, probability factorization and directed graphs, relevance-vector-machine graphical models, the noisy-OR representation, recursive Gaussian moments, d-separation and Markov blankets, collider effects and unreliable observations in a fuel-system example, enumeration of undirected graphs, local energy changes for ICM, a simplified latent-variable energy model, and pairwise distributions in a graphical model.

nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on graphical-model conditional independence, including the effect of observing a collider’s descendant and an unreliable fuel-gauge report; counting undirected graphs; locality of energy differences for iterated conditional modes; the most probable configuration when interaction and bias coefficients vanish; and the joint distribution of neighboring nodes in a graph.

nodes.summary: This passage presents Figure 8.54 and Exercises 8.10–8.24 on graphical-model independence, explaining how observing a collider’s descendant changes dependence; unreliable observations in a fuel-gauge model; enumeration of undirected graphs; local energy changes and MAP configurations in graphical models; tree distributions and directed/undirected equivalence; and sum-product message passing for chains and tree-structured factor graphs, including efficient inference, message ordering, connected-subset marginals, and equivalent expressions for variable and factor marginals.

nodes.title: 8.18 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 8.16–8.29 examine message passing and the sum-product algorithm on directed, undirected, and factor trees. They cover conditional inference, d-separation, equivalence and enumeration of tree representations, recovery of chain-model formulas, inductive proofs of valid message schedules, computation of variable, factor, subset, and pairwise marginals, alternative marginal identities, verification on a specific graph, a counterexample showing marginal modes need not form the joint mode, and the relationship between pending messages and graph cycles: cycles leave pending messages, whereas finite tree graphs eventually do not.

This section presents probabilistic graphical models as visual and computational frameworks built from probability sum and product rules. It covers directed Bayesian networks, conditional independence and d-separation, undirected Markov random fields, clique and energy factorizations, and relationships among directed, undirected, and chain graphs. Applications include regression, generative models, naive Bayes, image denoising, and code decoding. It develops exact and approximate inference through message passing, factor graphs, junction trees, dynamic programming, MAP methods, and loopy belief propagation, and concludes with Bayesian structure learning, model evidence, computational limitations, and extensive exercises on independence, graph construction, Gaussian models, noisy-OR and relevance-vector models, energy optimization, graph enumeration, and tree-based inference.

nodes.title: 9 Mixture Models and EM
9.1. K -means Clustering
9.1.1 Image segmentation and compression
nodes.summary: The text generalizes K-means to K-medoids using arbitrary dissimilarities, describing its hard-assignment E step, more costly prototype-selection M step, and motivation for probabilistic soft assignments. It illustrates K-means for RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression, including the compression formula, numerical image example, quality–compression trade-off, and the benefit of using pixel blocks. It then introduces Gaussian mixtures as weighted Gaussian sums and reformulates them with a 1-of-K latent variable whose mixing probabilities define the component assignments and joint distribution.

This section develops K-means clustering as an iterative minimization of squared distances between data points and K prototype centres: hard assignments to the nearest centre alternate with recomputation of centres as assigned-point means. It discusses the algorithm’s convergence and local-minimum limitation, illustrates it with Old Faithful data, and extends the ideas to K-medoids with arbitrary dissimilarities. Applications to RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression demonstrate quality–compression trade-offs and block coding. The section then introduces Gaussian mixtures and their 1-of-K latent-variable formulation, connecting K-means’ assignment and update steps to the E and M steps of the EM algorithm.

nodes.title: 9.2. Mixtures of Gaussians
9.2.1 Maximum likelihood
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian-mixture responsibilities, interpreting them as posterior component probabilities and explaining their use in sampling and visualizing complete, marginal, and softly labeled data. It formulates the i.i.d. mixture likelihood, discusses its singularities, collapse-induced overfitting, practical avoidance heuristics, and label-switching non-identifiability. Because direct maximization has no closed-form solution, it introduces EM and begins its derivation, obtaining the responsibility-weighted update for each component mean and defining the effective membership count N_k.

nodes.title: 9.2.2 EM for Gaussian mixtures
EM for Gaussian Mixtures
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for Gaussian mixtures through a visual progression of responsibility assignment and weighted parameter updates, noting its slower and more computationally intensive convergence than K-means, common K-means initialization practice, singularity precautions, and susceptibility to local maxima. It then gives the complete Gaussian-mixture EM algorithm—initialization, responsibility-based E step, weighted mean/covariance/mixing-coefficient M step, likelihood evaluation, and convergence testing—and introduces an alternative latent-variable view in which the observed-data likelihood is the logarithm of a sum or integral over hidden variables.

This section derives the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixtures from the likelihood equations: responsibilities provide effective cluster memberships, yielding weighted updates for component means, covariances, and mixing coefficients. Because these quantities depend on one another, EM iterates responsibility computation (E step) and parameter maximization (M step), monotonically improving likelihood until convergence. It illustrates the process on Old Faithful data and discusses initialization, computational behavior, singularity precautions, local maxima, and the broader latent-variable and variational-inference context.

The section first illustrates clustering-based image compression and its compression-quality trade-off, then introduces Gaussian mixtures through discrete 1-of-K latent variables, deriving their joint and marginal distributions. It develops responsibilities and the mixture likelihood, explains singularities, overfitting, and label non-identifiability, and derives the EM algorithm with weighted updates for component parameters. EM is presented as alternating responsibility estimation and likelihood maximization, illustrated on Old Faithful data, with discussion of initialization, convergence, safeguards, local optima, and links to latent-variable and variational methods.

nodes.title: 9.3. An Alternative View of EM
The General EM Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces EM as a method for maximizing likelihoods with latent or missing variables. It contrasts difficult incomplete-data likelihoods with tractable complete-data likelihoods, defines the E step posterior and expected complete-data log likelihood Q, and defines the M step that maximizes Q. It presents the full iterative algorithm, its monotonic likelihood-improvement property, and its MAP extension using a parameter prior. It also explains EM for missing data under a missing-at-random assumption and begins applying the latent-variable interpretation to Gaussian mixture models, where component labels form the missing information.

nodes.title: 9.3.1 Gaussian mixtures revisited
nodes.summary: The text presents the general EM procedure, including its E and M steps, convergence check, and MAP extension with parameter priors. It explains how EM applies to missing data under a missing-at-random assumption. It then revisits Gaussian mixtures using complete and incomplete data: complete-data likelihood maximization has simple closed-form solutions, while replacing unknown indicators with their posterior expectations produces responsibilities and the standard EM updates for mixture parameters. Finally, it introduces the connection to K-means, contrasting EM's soft assignments with K-means' hard assignments and beginning to show K-means as a limiting case of EM with shared isotropic covariances.

nodes.title: 9.3.2 Relation to K -means
nodes.summary: The text derives the Gaussian-mixture EM algorithm from the posterior over latent assignments, showing posterior factorization, identifying responsibilities, and expressing the expected complete-data log likelihood used in the E and M steps. It then demonstrates that K-means is the zero-variance, hard-assignment limit of EM for mixtures with shared isotropic covariances, with the likelihood objective reducing to the K-means distortion measure, and briefly introduces Bernoulli mixture models (latent class analysis) as an extension to discrete data and a foundation for hidden Markov models.

nodes.title: 9.3.3 Mixtures of Bernoulli distributions
nodes.summary: The text first establishes K-means as the zero-variance limit of EM for an isotropic Gaussian mixture: responsibilities become nearest-centroid hard assignments, mean updates match K-means, mixing coefficients equal assignment fractions, and the expected complete-data likelihood becomes the negative distortion objective. It then develops mixtures of Bernoulli distributions for binary data, deriving their moments, latent-variable formulation, likelihood, EM responsibilities, weighted parameter updates, and mixing-coefficient updates. The discussion covers likelihood singularities, an application to clustering binarized handwritten digits, Bayesian beta/Dirichlet priors, and multinomial extensions. Finally, it introduces EM as an alternative method for Bayesian linear-regression evidence optimization by treating the regression weights as latent variables and re-estimating the hyperparameters alpha and beta.

nodes.title: 9.3.4 EM for Bayesian linear regression
nodes.summary: The text reviews Bernoulli mixture models and their extensions with priors, then presents EM formulations for Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector regression, including posterior expectations and hyperparameter re-estimation equations equivalent to evidence maximization. It concludes by introducing the general EM framework for latent-variable models through the likelihood decomposition into a lower-bound functional and a KL divergence, setting up the proof and broader variational interpretation of EM.

This section presents EM as an iterative method for maximum-likelihood or MAP estimation in latent-variable and missing-data models. It develops the E-step/M-step framework, convergence behavior, and missing-at-random interpretation; applies the method to Gaussian mixtures and relates it to K-means; extends it to Bernoulli and multinomial mixtures with priors and applications; applies it to Bayesian and relevance-vector linear regression for evidence optimization; and concludes with an abstract lower-bound and KL-divergence interpretation that explains EM's variational foundation.

nodes.title: 9.4. The EM Algorithm in General
nodes.summary: The text transitions from mixture-model re-estimation equations to a general treatment of EM. It discusses factorization for iid data, exponential-family simplifications, graphical interpretations, MAP-EM with priors, GEM and ECM extensions, partial E-step optimization, and incremental EM with sufficient-statistic updates and convergence behavior. It also references relevant exercises and introduces exercises on finite K-means convergence and stochastic K-means.

nodes.title: 10 Approximate Inference
10.1. Variational Inference
10.1.1 Factorized distributions
Leonhard Euler
nodes.summary: The text derives the mean-field variational inference update for a factorized approximation: maximizing the lower bound with respect to one factor reduces to minimizing a KL divergence, yielding an optimal factor whose log is the expectation of the joint log distribution over all other factors, plus a normalization constant. Because the updates are mutually dependent, the factors are updated iteratively by coordinate ascent, with convergence ensured by convexity in each factor. It then begins discussing the properties and inaccuracies of factorized approximations through a correlated two-dimensional Gaussian example, and includes a biographical note on Leonhard Euler and his major mathematical achievements.

This section introduces mean-field variational inference, restricting the approximation to a product of distributions over disjoint variable groups. It derives the optimal factor update through KL minimization and expectations of the joint log distribution, explains iterative coordinate-ascent optimization and its convergence properties, and begins illustrating the inaccuracies caused by factorization with a correlated Gaussian example, alongside a note on Leonhard Euler's mathematical achievements.

nodes.title: 10.1.2 Properties of factorized approximations
nodes.summary: The text derives coordinate-wise optimal factors for mean-field variational inference and explains their coupled coordinate-ascent solution. It analyzes factorization error using a correlated Gaussian, showing that minimizing KL(q||p) preserves the mean but produces overly compact, variance-underestimating approximations. It contrasts this with minimizing KL(p||q), which yields exact marginals for factorized factors, covers broader support, and behaves differently for multimodal distributions. The alpha-divergence family and its zero-forcing, zero-avoiding, and Hellinger-related cases are introduced. Finally, a factorized variational treatment of a univariate Gaussian model with Gaussian-Gamma priors is set up.

nodes.title: 10.1.3 Example: The univariate Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text first reviews α-divergences, their KL limits, nonnegativity, and the contrasting zero-forcing and zero-avoiding behavior of different α values, including the symmetric Hellinger-related case. It then develops a factorized variational approximation for the posterior of the mean and precision of a univariate Gaussian with Gaussian-Gamma conjugate priors. The optimal factors are derived as Gaussian and gamma distributions whose parameters depend on moments of the other factor, motivating alternating iterative updates; the exact posterior, convergence illustration, large-sample behavior, and a simplified noninformative-prior formulation are discussed. The excerpt ends while deriving explicit moment equations for that simplified case.

This section introduces variational inference as a deterministic approach to approximating intractable posteriors and evidences. It reviews the calculus of variations, formulates the evidence lower bound and its KL-divergence decomposition, and explains why unrestricted optimization is exact while restricted distributions yield approximations. It then develops mean-field factorized approximations and coordinate-ascent updates, analyzes their convergence and errors through correlated-Gaussian examples, contrasts forward and reverse KL behavior, and introduces alpha-divergences. Finally, it applies factorized variational inference to a univariate Gaussian with unknown mean and precision, deriving coupled Gaussian and gamma factors, iterative moment updates, exact and asymptotic comparisons, and a noninformative-prior special case.

This section motivates approximate inference by describing the need to compute latent-variable posteriors and expectations, particularly in EM and Bayesian models, and by explaining why high dimensionality, complex distributions, and intractable integrals make exact inference impractical. It then develops variational inference, including the variational calculus, evidence lower bound, KL-divergence interpretation, mean-field factorization, coordinate-ascent optimization, convergence and error behavior, divergence comparisons, and alpha-divergences. A detailed Gaussian example with unknown mean and precision illustrates the resulting Gaussian and gamma factors, iterative moment updates, exact and asymptotic accuracy comparisons, and the noninformative-prior case.

Appendix C compiles a broad treatment of probabilistic and statistical machine learning, beginning with probability foundations, Gaussian and related distributions, Bayesian inference, maximum likelihood, sequential estimation, periodic variables, mixtures, exponential families, and nonparametric methods. It then develops linear regression and classification, neural networks, kernel and sparse kernel machines, graphical models, mixture models with EM, and variational approximate inference. Across these topics it covers mathematical derivations, geometry, matrix identities, conjugate and approximate Bayesian methods, optimization, regularization, uncertainty, model comparison, sparsity, latent-variable inference, computational limitations, and practical modeling choices. Extensive exercises address distributional identities and moments, entropy and KL divergence, Gaussian and matrix properties, estimation, regression and classification, kernel and neural models, graphical inference, EM, and variational techniques.

nodes.title: Appendix B
10.1.4 Model comparison
nodes.summary: The text completes a variational Gaussian inference example by deriving the unbiased Bayesian variance estimator, then develops variational model comparison using q(Z,m)=q(Z|m)q(m), a model-specific evidence lower bound, and q(m) ∝ p(m)exp(L_m), with latent distributions optimized separately by model. It then introduces variational inference for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, defining the latent assignments, mixture and data likelihoods, use of precision matrices, and conjugate priors including a symmetric Dirichlet prior over the mixing coefficients.

nodes.title: 10.2. Illustration: Variational Mixture of Gaussians
10.2.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian inference for a Gaussian mixture model. It specifies Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors, presents the graphical-model interpretation, derives a variational factorization and coordinate updates, and shows that the assignment distributions yield normalized responsibilities. Responsibility-weighted sufficient statistics then update Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart posteriors, with explicit formulas for all required expectations and responsibility calculations. The resulting algorithm alternates variational E- and M-like steps, closely paralleling EM while accounting for parameter uncertainty. An Old Faithful example illustrates automatic component suppression and the effect of the Dirichlet concentration prior. The Bayesian method avoids EM singularities and overfitting and can infer an effective number of components. Finally, the text introduces the variational lower bound, explains its use for convergence and implementation checks, and gives its decomposition and initial evaluated terms.

nodes.title: 10.2.2 Variational lower bound
nodes.summary: The text explains the benefits of priors and variational inference for Gaussian mixtures, including removal of singularities, avoidance of overfitting with many components, and automatic component-number selection. It presents the variational lower bound, its role in convergence and implementation checks, its decomposition into likelihood, prior, and entropy terms with explicit component formulas, and its use for deriving update equations. It then defines the predictive density for a new observation by summing over its latent component and integrating over the posterior parameter distribution.

nodes.title: 10.2.3 Predictive density
nodes.summary: The passage completes the variational lower-bound expressions for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture, explains their entropy terms and their use in deriving variational updates, then derives the approximate predictive density as a mixture of Student’s t-distributions that becomes Gaussian-like with large data. It concludes by discussing selection of the number of components and the Bayesian significance of label-switching symmetry, whereby K! parameter configurations represent the same mixture density.

nodes.title: 10.2.4 Determining the number of components
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational predictive distribution for a Gaussian mixture, showing that it is a mixture of Student’s t-distributions that approaches a Gaussian mixture with large data. It explains how to determine the number of components while accounting for K! label-switching modes through an ln K! correction, illustrates this with the Old Faithful data, and contrasts Bayesian model comparison with maximum likelihood. It also presents an alternative point-estimation method for mixing weights that automatically prunes irrelevant components. Finally, it discusses induced factorizations in the optimal variational posterior, their computational importance, and a d-separation criterion for detecting when further factorization occurs.

nodes.title: 10.2.5 Induced factorizations
nodes.summary: The text explains automatic relevance determination for pruning unnecessary Gaussian-mixture components and develops the concept of induced factorizations, showing how conditional independencies and d-separation determine further factorization of variational posteriors and improve implementation efficiency. It then introduces variational Bayesian linear regression: a Gaussian likelihood and weight prior with known noise precision, a gamma hyperprior on the weight precision, the resulting joint model and graphical representation, and the goal of approximating the posterior over weights and hyperparameters.

This section develops variational Bayesian inference for Gaussian mixture models, beginning with their latent-variable likelihood and conjugate Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart priors. It derives the factorized variational posterior, responsibility and parameter updates, sufficient statistics, and an EM-like iterative algorithm that accounts for parameter uncertainty. The method is illustrated on Old Faithful data, showing automatic component suppression and protection against singularities and overfitting. The variational lower bound is decomposed and used for convergence checks and update derivations. Predictive inference produces a Student's t mixture, and Bayesian model comparison addresses component-number selection and label-switching. The section also covers relevance-based pruning, induced posterior factorizations identified through conditional independence and d-separation, and extends the discussion by introducing the variational Bayesian linear regression model.

nodes.title: 10.3. Variational Linear Regression
10.3.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text first explains how d-separation can establish independence between variational factors, illustrating this with a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model. It then develops mean-field variational inference for Bayesian linear regression with fixed noise precision, a Gaussian weight prior controlled by a gamma-distributed precision hyperparameter, and factorization q(w,α)=q(w)q(α). The resulting updates are a gamma distribution for α and a Gaussian distribution for w, with moments used in alternating coordinate updates. In the uninformative-hyperprior limit, the method coincides with the evidence/EM approach. Finally, it derives the Gaussian predictive distribution for a new input by marginalizing the likelihood over q(w).

nodes.title: 10.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational Gaussian posterior for regression weights and the expected precision and weight moments, explains alternating updates for q(w) and q(alpha), and shows that with an infinitely broad alpha prior the variational method coincides with evidence maximization using EM apart from replacing alpha by its expectation. It derives the Gaussian predictive distribution with input-dependent variance, defines the variational lower bound, lists its likelihood, prior, and entropy contributions, and demonstrates that the bound supports selecting the correct polynomial model while avoiding the overfitting favored by maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 10.3.3 Lower bound
nodes.summary: The passage completes variational linear regression by giving the predictive variance and the variational evidence lower bound, including formulas for all expected likelihood, prior, and entropy terms. It explains how the bound supports model selection, correctly identifying a degree-three polynomial and avoiding maximum-likelihood overfitting. It then introduces exponential-family distributions and conjugate priors, distinguishing observed data, extensive latent variables, and fixed-dimensional parameters, and gives the general exponential-family forms for an iid joint distribution and its conjugate prior.

This section develops mean-field variational inference for Bayesian linear regression, deriving Gaussian weight and gamma precision factors, their alternating updates, predictive mean and variance, and the evidence lower bound with likelihood, prior, and entropy terms. It relates the method to evidence maximization and EM in the uninformative-prior limit, shows how the bound enables appropriate polynomial model selection without maximum-likelihood overfitting, and concludes by introducing exponential-family distributions, conjugate priors, and the roles of observed, latent, and parameter variables.

nodes.title: 10.4. Exponential Family Distributions
10.4.1 Variational message passing
nodes.summary: The text derives mean-field variational inference for exponential-family models, showing that latent-variable factors become independent across observations while the parameter factor retains a conjugate exponential-family form. Their coupled updates alternate between expected sufficient-statistic computation and expected natural-parameter computation. It then generalizes variational inference to directed graphical models: factor updates depend only on each node’s Markov blanket, enabling local computations and general-purpose implementations. For conjugate-exponential networks, these updates become distributed local message passing, which also facilitates lower-bound evaluation and scales effectively to large graphs.

This section introduces variational inference for models whose complete-data distributions and priors form conjugate exponential families. It distinguishes latent variables from fixed-dimensional parameters, sets out the exponential-family likelihood and conjugate prior, and derives mean-field updates that alternate between expected sufficient statistics and expected natural parameters. It then extends the method to directed graphical models, where Markov-blanket-based local updates yield distributed variational message passing, efficient lower-bound computation, and good scalability.

nodes.title: 10.5. Local Variational Methods
nodes.summary: The text develops local variational inference through convex and concave bounds and convex duality. It derives tangent-line representations and conjugate functions, first for exp(-x), then gives the corresponding concave-function relations and explains transformations for nonconvex functions. Applying these ideas to the logistic sigmoid yields both an exponential upper bound based on the binary entropy conjugate and the Jaakkola–Jordan Gaussian lower bound, obtained by transforming the log sigmoid into a function of x². The text discusses the bounds’ graphical behavior, their usefulness for analytically approximating sigmoid–Gaussian integrals, optimization of the variational parameter, limitations for the multiclass softmax, and the fact that optimized bounds are generally not exact. It then introduces variational Bayesian logistic regression, emphasizing its rigorous evidence lower bound and improved flexibility over Laplace approximation, and sets up the marginal likelihood and binary likelihood factorization to apply the sigmoid bound.

nodes.title: 10.6. Variational Logistic Regression
10.6.1 Variational posterior distribution
nodes.summary: This section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using the Jaakkola–Jordan local quadratic bound on the sigmoid. Each training example receives a variational parameter, producing a quadratic likelihood bound whose combination with a Gaussian prior yields a Gaussian variational posterior with explicitly defined mean and covariance. The variational parameters are optimized by maximizing a rigorous marginal-likelihood lower bound, either through EM or direct optimization after analytic integration over the weights. The approach is more flexible and often more accurate than Laplace approximation, supports batch and sequential learning, and is directly applicable only to binary classification.

nodes.title: 10.6.2 Optimizing the variational parameters
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using a quadratic bound, producing a Gaussian posterior whose parameters depend on local variational variables ξ_n. It explains optimizing these variables through EM or equivalent direct maximization, gives the ξ re-estimation rule and closed-form lower bound, and discusses batch and sequential learning, predictive inference, binary-class limitations, and the illustrative behavior of the resulting decision boundaries. It concludes by introducing variational inference for estimating the prior hyperparameter α through a combined global-local approximation.

nodes.title: 10.6.3 Inference of hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text presents a variational Bayesian treatment of logistic regression, including predictive behavior, sequential posterior updating, and its relation to large-margin classification. It then develops inference of the Gaussian-prior precision hyperparameter using a gamma hyperprior, local and global variational bounds, factorized distributions, Gaussian and gamma update formulas, local-parameter re-estimation, and an iterative update scheme. Finally, it introduces expectation propagation, contrasting its reverse-KL objective with variational inference and showing that EP matches sufficient-statistic moments between the target and exponential-family approximation.

This section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression from the Jaakkola–Jordan quadratic sigmoid bound, deriving a Gaussian approximate posterior and a tractable marginal-likelihood lower bound. It covers EM and direct optimization of local variational parameters, batch and sequential updates, prediction, binary-class limitations, decision-boundary behavior, and comparisons with Laplace and large-margin methods. It then extends inference to the Gaussian-prior precision using a gamma hyperprior and global–local variational updates, and concludes with expectation propagation, its reverse-KL objective, and exponential-family moment matching.

nodes.title: 10.7. Expectation Propagation
Expectation Propagation
nodes.summary: The text completes the derivation of EP factor normalization, presents the full expectation-propagation algorithm for posterior and evidence approximation, and discusses its ADF special case, convergence properties, energy-function interpretation, and differences from variational Bayes. It then introduces a Gaussian-mixture clutter problem in which exact inference is exponentially difficult, and explains how EP represents the prior and likelihood factors using a spherical Gaussian approximation for the unknown mean.

nodes.title: 10.7.1 Example: The clutter problem
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates expectation propagation using a Gaussian mean-estimation problem contaminated by Gaussian clutter. The exact posterior contains exponentially many Gaussian components, so EP approximates the prior and observation factors with Gaussian or exponential-quadratic terms and iteratively performs cavity removal, tilted-distribution normalization, moment matching, and factor refinement. It gives the resulting update equations, interprets the non-clutter responsibility, specifies initialization and convergence, and presents an approximate evidence formula. It also discusses unusual negative or infinite factor variance parameters, illustrates the approximation graphically, compares EP with variational Bayes and Laplace methods, and introduces the extension of EP to factor graphs with factors involving variable subsets.

nodes.title: 10.7.2 Expectation propagation on graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the clutter-problem discussion by giving the EP evidence approximation, illustrating factor approximations, explaining that unusual factor variances can be harmless, and comparing EP with variational Bayes and Laplace methods. It then develops EP on factor graphs, showing through a concrete example and a general derivation that fully factorized EP is equivalent to sum-product or loopy belief propagation, with sequential updates reproducing standard schedules and exact inference on trees. It discusses partially disconnected or grouped approximations, the open problem of selecting such structures, and the unifying role of alpha-divergences across message-passing methods. The excerpt ends with exercises on variational decompositions, moment matching, factorized KL minimization, and Gaussian KL optimization.

The section finishes the preceding variational Bayes updates and then develops expectation propagation as reverse-KL, moment-matching inference with exponential-family factor approximations. It presents the EP cavity, tilted-distribution, factor-refinement, normalization, convergence, evidence, and energy interpretations; applies the method in detail to a Gaussian clutter problem and compares it with variational Bayes and Laplace methods; and generalizes EP to factor graphs, where fully factorized EP recovers belief propagation and is exact on trees. It also discusses grouped approximations, alpha-divergences, and related exercises.

It discusses a unified alpha-divergence framework for variational message passing, belief propagation, expectation propagation, and related algorithms. It then lists exercises on the KL decomposition of log evidence, solving for factor means, deriving variational factors with Lagrange multipliers, and optimizing Gaussian approximations, with the final exercise truncated.

It presents sum-product as the fully factorized special case of expectation propagation, discusses partially disconnected or grouped-factor approximations for improved accuracy, and identifies the open problem of selecting the best structure. It then places variational message passing, expectation propagation, belief propagation, and several other message-passing methods within the alpha-divergence framework. nodes.title: 10.5 ( ) www

nodes.title: 10.10 ( ) www

These cover the equivalence between point-estimate variational optimization and EM, the limiting relationships between alpha divergences and the two KL divergences, derivation and asymptotic behavior of Gaussian mean and precision variational factors, calculation of the reciprocal expected precision, a variational model-posterior decomposition, optimization of model probabilities under normalization, and derivation of the optimal latent-variable factor for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model.

nodes.title: 10.11 ( ) www

They derive posterior distributions and parameter updates, expected mixing coefficients, and all terms of the variational lower bound; obtain the re-estimation equations and predictive distribution; demonstrate that the large-sample variational solution converges to the EM maximum-likelihood solution, including concentrated posteriors, matching responsibilities, and a Gaussian-mixture predictive distribution; and count the K! equivalent parameter configurations caused by component-label permutations.

They also analyze concavity and dual variational bounds for logarithmic and logistic functions, extend variational regression with a gamma precision hyperprior, and derive assumed-density-filtering and EP evidence and moment-update formulas.

nodes.title: 11 Sampling Methods
11.1. Basic Sampling Algorithms
11.1.1 Standard distributions
nodes.summary: The text introduces basic sampling methods, assuming a source of uniform pseudo-random numbers. It explains inverse-transform sampling using the cumulative distribution, with exponential and Cauchy examples, extends the method through Jacobians to multiple variables, and details the Box-Muller procedure for generating standard and general Gaussian samples, including multivariate Gaussians via Cholesky decomposition. Because transformation methods are restricted to distributions with tractable invertible integrals, the text motivates rejection and importance sampling, then begins rejection sampling for an unnormalized target distribution and an easily sampled proposal distribution.

nodes.title: 11.1.2 Rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text completes the Gaussian transformation method, showing how independent standard normals are obtained, how to form univariate and multivariate Gaussians using scaling, shifting, and Cholesky factorization, and why more general sampling methods are needed. It then explains rejection sampling for distributions known up to normalization: samples are drawn from an enveloping proposal and accepted according to the target-to-envelope ratio, with efficiency determined by the envelope areas. A shifted and scaled Cauchy proposal is presented for gamma sampling, including parameters minimizing rejection. Finally, adaptive rejection sampling is introduced, using tangent-line envelopes for log-concave distributions and refining them with rejected samples.

nodes.title: 11.1.3 Adaptive rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of rejection sampling with a gamma-distribution example using a scaled Cauchy proposal and gives the parameter choices that minimize rejection. It then introduces adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave targets: tangent lines built from grid-point evaluations create a piecewise exponential envelope, rejected samples refine it, derivative-free variants are possible, and a Metropolis-Hastings extension handles non-log-concave distributions. Rejection sampling is shown to suffer exponential loss of acceptance in high dimensions, even with closely matched Gaussian proposals, making it primarily a low-dimensional or subroutine method. Finally, importance sampling is introduced as a way to estimate expectations without directly sampling from the target, using samples from an accessible proposal distribution and weighting them by target-to-proposal density ratios; uniform-grid approaches are rejected as exponentially inefficient in high-dimensional, concentrated distributions.

nodes.title: 11.1.4 Importance sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains importance sampling as a way to estimate expectations under difficult distributions by sampling from an easier proposal and applying importance weights, including the self-normalized formulation when density normalizers are unknown. It contrasts this with inefficient uniform-grid integration and notes the dimensionality limitations of rejection sampling. It discusses the method’s dependence on proposal coverage, weight degeneracy, reduced effective sample size, and the possibility of undetected severe errors. Applications to discrete graphical models include uniform sampling, likelihood-weighted ancestral sampling, and adaptive self-importance sampling. The section concludes by introducing sampling-importance-resampling and the difficulty of selecting the rejection-sampling constant.

nodes.title: 11.1.5 Sampling-importance-resampling
nodes.summary: The text discusses limitations and graphical-model implementations of importance sampling, including weight degeneracy, undetected bias, proposal-distribution requirements, uniform sampling, likelihood weighting, and adaptive self-importance sampling. It then presents sampling-importance-resampling, its weighted-resampling procedure, convergence justification, dependence on the proposal distribution, and use of original weighted samples for moment estimates. Finally, it explains Monte Carlo EM, its sampled approximation to the E step, extension to MAP estimation, and stochastic EM for mixture models.

nodes.title: 11.1.6 Sampling and the EM algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains weighted importance-sampling estimates and then describes Monte Carlo EM, in which posterior samples of hidden variables approximate the EM E-step, with an extension to MAP estimation by adding the parameter prior and a stochastic-EM mixture-model variant using single-sample hard assignments. It introduces Bayesian data augmentation through alternating imputation and posterior steps to sample latent variables and parameters when joint posterior sampling is difficult. Finally, it motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo as a more powerful general sampling framework than rejection or importance sampling, especially in high-dimensional settings.

This section develops basic sampling algorithms, beginning with transformation methods based on uniform random numbers, inverse cumulative distributions, Jacobians, and Box–Muller and Cholesky procedures for Gaussian samples. It then covers rejection sampling and adaptive rejection sampling, including proposal construction, efficiency, gamma examples, log-concave envelopes, and high-dimensional limitations. Importance sampling is presented for expectation estimation with known or unknown normalization constants, together with proposal requirements, weight degeneracy, graphical-model applications, and sampling-importance-resampling. The section concludes with Monte Carlo, MAP, and stochastic EM, Bayesian data augmentation, and the motivation for Markov chain Monte Carlo in complex high-dimensional settings.

nodes.title: 11.2. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
11.2.1 Markov chains
nodes.summary: The text explains why ordinary random walks explore state spaces inefficiently, then develops the theory needed for Markov chain Monte Carlo. It defines Markov chains, transition kernels, homogeneity, invariant and equilibrium distributions, detailed balance, reversibility, and ergodicity, and describes constructing composite transitions by mixtures or successive base updates. It then introduces and proves the invariance of the generalized Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for asymmetric proposals, notes its independence from the target normalization constant and its reduction to Metropolis for symmetric proposals, and begins discussing how proposal variance affects performance. A figure illustrates Gaussian Metropolis sampling and reports accepted and rejected candidate moves.

nodes.title: 11.2.2 The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how mixtures and sequential compositions of Markov transitions preserve invariance, when they preserve detailed balance, and how symmetric ordering can restore it. It then presents the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for nonsymmetric proposals, including its acceptance probability, detailed-balance proof, and independence from the target normalization constant. It discusses the impact of Gaussian proposal scale and distribution anisotropy on acceptance, random-walk behavior, and convergence. Finally, it introduces Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update MCMC method and a special case of Metropolis-Hastings.

This section begins with Bayesian data augmentation, alternating imputation of hidden variables with posterior parameter updates, and then develops Markov chain Monte Carlo as a general method for sampling difficult, especially high-dimensional, posterior distributions. It explains state-dependent proposals, the Metropolis algorithm and its acceptance rule, repeated states, convergence, correlation, and thinning; develops the underlying theory of Markov chains, invariant distributions, detailed balance, reversibility, ergodicity, and composite transitions; and generalizes the method to Metropolis-Hastings for asymmetric proposals. The section also discusses proposal-scale and target-geometry effects on efficiency and convergence, illustrates Gaussian sampling, and introduces Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update special case of Metropolis-Hastings.

nodes.title: 11.3. Gibbs Sampling
Josiah Willard Gibbs
nodes.summary: Gibbs sampling is a sequential conditional-update Markov-chain method whose joint target distribution is invariant, provided the chain is ergodic; initialization, autocorrelation, and subsampling affect practical use. It is equivalent to always-accepted Metropolis-Hastings, can mix slowly for correlated Gaussians, and may be improved through over-relaxation or blocking. Its applicability depends on sampling graphical-model full conditionals, which are simplified by Markov blankets, conjugacy, and log-concavity; replacing draws by modes gives ICM. The passage concludes by introducing slice sampling, an auxiliary-variable method with automatically adapted step size.

The section motivates Gibbs sampling by explaining the slow convergence of isotropic Metropolis-Hastings proposals on highly anisotropic, correlated distributions. It then presents Gibbs sampling as sequential draws from full conditional distributions, explains its invariance, ergodicity, relation to always-accepted Metropolis-Hastings, and practical issues such as initialization, autocorrelation, subsampling, and slow mixing. It discusses improvements through over-relaxation and blocking, conditions that make full conditionals tractable in graphical models—including Markov blankets, conjugacy, and log-concavity—and the deterministic ICM variant obtained by using conditional modes. Finally, it introduces slice sampling as an auxiliary-variable alternative with automatically adapted step sizes.

nodes.title: 11.4. Slice Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains refinements of Gibbs sampling, including conditional sampling via Markov blankets, adaptive rejection sampling for suitable conditionals, ICM as a greedy mode-based alternative, and blocking to reduce dependence between samples. It then presents slice sampling, which introduces an auxiliary variable to sample uniformly under the unnormalized target density and uses an adaptive bracket-expansion and shrinkage procedure when direct slice sampling is impractical; the method also extends componentwise to multivariate distributions. Finally, it introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based, Hamiltonian-dynamics approach for continuous distributions that enables large, low-rejection moves, beginning with the formulation of momentum variables and first-order dynamical equations.

nodes.title: 11.5. The Hybrid Monte Carlo Algorithm
11.5.1 Dynamical systems
William Hamilton
nodes.summary: The text develops the foundations of hybrid Monte Carlo by augmenting position variables with momenta and defining potential, kinetic, and total Hamiltonian energy. Hamilton’s equations conserve the Hamiltonian, while Liouville’s theorem ensures phase-space volume preservation, making the distribution proportional to exp(-H) invariant. Continuous Hamiltonian evolution enables large, systematic moves without random-walk behavior but is not ergodic because energy is fixed, so Gaussian momentum resampling is alternated with the dynamics. Since numerical integration introduces error, the volume-preserving leapfrog scheme is presented, along with its half-step momentum and full-step position updates; remaining errors are addressed later in the HMC algorithm. The section also highlights the advantage of using gradient information over basic Metropolis sampling and provides a sidebar biography of William Rowan Hamilton.

This section develops the dynamical-systems foundation of hybrid Monte Carlo. It augments position variables with momenta and formulates their evolution using Hamiltonian mechanics, defining potential, kinetic, and total energy. Conservation of the Hamiltonian and Liouville volume preservation establish an invariant phase-space distribution, while the resulting trajectories permit large, gradient-informed moves instead of random walks. Because fixed-energy trajectories are not ergodic, momenta are resampled between trajectories. The section then introduces the reversible, volume-preserving leapfrog method for numerical integration, noting that its energy errors will later be corrected by a Metropolis step, and includes a biography of William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.5.2 Hybrid Monte Carlo
nodes.summary: The text explains Hybrid Monte Carlo as a Metropolis-corrected leapfrog method that removes discretization bias through momentum refreshment, reversible forward/backward trajectories, and volume preservation, thereby satisfying detailed balance. It discusses possible non-ergodic periodic trajectories and random step-size selection as a remedy. For Gaussian targets, it derives the required step-size and trajectory-length scaling and contrasts HMC’s efficiency with random-walk Metropolis. It then introduces partition functions as normalization constants and Bayesian model-evidence measures, explains why their ratios matter for model comparison, and gives an importance-sampling estimator for ratios of partition functions using a reference energy function.

The section develops Hybrid Monte Carlo from Hamiltonian dynamics, showing how momentum augmentation, conserved energy, volume preservation, and leapfrog integration produce efficient gradient-informed proposals. It explains momentum refreshment, Metropolis correction, reversibility, detailed balance, and remedies for non-ergodic trajectories, including random step sizes, with scaling results for Gaussian targets and comparisons to random-walk Metropolis. It also introduces partition functions and their ratios for normalization and Bayesian model comparison, along with an importance-sampling estimator, and includes a biography of William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.6. Estimating the Partition Function
nodes.summary: The text compares the efficiency of leapfrog-based hybrid Monte Carlo with random-walk Metropolis, showing that HMC scales linearly rather than quadratically with the ratio of the largest to smallest relevant length scales. It then explains partition functions as normalization constants and model evidences, derives their ratios through importance sampling, discusses limitations caused by poor distributional overlap, and presents Markov-chain-based importance sampling and chaining through interpolating intermediate energy distributions to estimate difficult partition functions. The section concludes with ten exercises covering estimator moments, inverse-transform sampling, Cauchy and Gaussian generation, change-of-variables proofs, rejection sampling, adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, and the mean-square behavior of a simple random walk.
