nodes.title: 11.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sampling methods, covering estimator expectation and variance, inverse-transform sampling, transformations for Cauchy and other distributions, Gaussian generation through Cholesky factorization, a proof of rejection sampling correctness, adaptive rejection sampling envelopes and algorithms, and the second-moment behavior of a simple random walk.

nodes.title: 11.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sampling methods, covering Monte Carlo estimator moments, inverse-transform sampling, transformations for Cauchy and multivariate Gaussian distributions, polar-variable transformations, rejection sampling correctness, adaptive rejection sampling envelopes and algorithms, random-walk moments, Gibbs sampling detailed balance and ergodicity, derivation of Gibbs conditionals in a Gaussian–gamma model, over-relaxation moments, equivalence of Hamiltonian and standard sampling equations, and the Gaussian form of a conditional distribution.

nodes.title: 11.11 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 11.11–11.16 on Gibbs sampling, ergodicity, Gaussian-gamma conditional distributions, over-relaxation, Hamiltonian dynamics, and Gaussian conditional distributions. It includes figures illustrating a disconnected uniform distribution over z1 and z2 and a three-node model for an observed Gaussian variable x with unknown mean μ and precision τ.

nodes.title: 11.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents two figures illustrating a disconnected uniform distribution over z1 and z2 and a Gaussian observation model with unknown mean and precision, followed by exercises on Gibbs sampling, detailed balance, ergodicity, conditional posterior derivations, over-relaxation moments, equivalence of Hamiltonian and alternative update equations, and proving that a specified conditional distribution is Gaussian.

nodes.title: 11.16 ( ) By making use of (11.56), (11.57), and (11.63), show that the conditional distribution p(r|z) is a Gaussian.
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gibbs sampling, ergodicity, conditional distributions, over-relaxation, and Hamiltonian dynamics. It includes a disconnected uniform distribution over shaded regions for assessing Gibbs-sampling ergodicity, a Gaussian observation model with normal and gamma priors for deriving Gibbs conditionals, verification of the moments of an over-relaxation update, demonstrations of equivalence between Hamiltonian and earlier update equations, and a proof that a specified conditional distribution is Gaussian.

nodes.title: 11.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes a hybrid Monte Carlo detailed-balance exercise and begins the chapter on continuous latent variables. It explains why high-dimensional data may lie near low-dimensional, often nonlinear manifolds, illustrating this with transformed digit images and oil-flow measurements, and describes generative latent-variable models with noise. It introduces linear-Gaussian models, probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, their estimation and extensions, then develops standard PCA through its maximum-variance and minimum-error formulations. PCA is characterized by the leading eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix, with computational considerations, and the text begins the orthonormal-basis derivation of its lower-dimensional approximation.

This section presents Monte Carlo methods for approximate inference, beginning with independent-sample expectation estimation and direct sampling in graphical models, then covering transformation, rejection, adaptive rejection, and importance sampling. It develops MCMC through Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs sampling, including convergence theory, mixing, dependence, blocking, over-relaxation, ICM, and slice sampling. It then introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as an efficient gradient-based method and explains estimation of partition functions and model evidences. Exercises reinforce sampling theory and algorithms, Gibbs and Hamiltonian methods, and Gaussian conditional derivations, while the closing material transitions to continuous latent-variable models and PCA.

Appendix B consolidates variational and sampling-based approximate inference. It completes foundational Gaussian variational calculations and model comparison, develops variational Bayesian Gaussian mixtures and linear and logistic regression, and establishes exponential-family, graphical-model, local-bound, message-passing, and expectation-propagation frameworks. It covers predictive inference, evidence lower bounds, model selection, asymptotics, pruning, label symmetry, hyperpriors, sequential updates, and extensive derivational exercises. The appendix then introduces Monte Carlo inference, from direct and importance sampling through Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs, slice, and hybrid Monte Carlo, including convergence, mixing, evidence estimation, and supporting exercises.

nodes.title: Appendix C
12.1.2 Minimum-error formulation
nodes.summary: The text explains PCA as the selection of covariance-matrix eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues to maximize variance in an M-dimensional projection, including computational costs and efficient partial-decomposition methods. It then gives the equivalent minimum-reconstruction-error formulation: represent data in an orthonormal basis, optimize the retained coordinates and mean-related offsets, and show that the optimal reconstruction is an orthogonal projection onto the eigenvector subspace. The minimum error is the sum of the omitted eigenvalues, so the retained directions are those of greatest variance; the method also covers the no-reduction case M=D and has non-unique directions for equal eigenvalues. CCA is introduced as a related method for finding highly correlated paired subspaces, and PCA application to compression of handwritten-digit data is begun.

nodes.title: 12.1.3 Applications of peA
nodes.summary: The text derives PCA from covariance-matrix eigenvectors, proving that the principal subspace consists of the directions of largest variance and that minimum distortion equals the sum of omitted eigenvalues. It discusses the equal-eigenvalue and no-reduction cases, relates PCA to CCA, and presents applications in digit-image compression, reconstruction, standardization, whitening, visualization, and comparison with Fisher’s discriminant. It concludes by explaining why conventional PCA is difficult when dimensionality exceeds the number of data points, due to zero eigenvalues and the cubic cost of direct eigendecomposition, motivating an alternative high-dimensional formulation.

nodes.title: 12.1.4 peA for high-dimensional data
nodes.summary: The text contrasts PCA with Fisher’s linear discriminant, showing that PCA maximizes variance but may mix classes, whereas the supervised discriminant improves separation, and illustrates airflow data projected onto principal components. It then explains an efficient PCA method for high-dimensional data when the sample count is below the feature dimension: the covariance eigendecomposition is replaced by an N×N eigenproblem, reducing cost from O(D³) to O(N³), after which the original eigenvectors are reconstructed and normalized. Finally, it introduces probabilistic PCA as a maximum-likelihood latent-variable formulation that uses a constrained Gaussian model with fewer parameters while retaining dominant data correlations.

nodes.title: 12.2. Probabilistic peA
12.2.1 Maximum likelihood peA
nodes.summary: The text develops maximum likelihood probabilistic PCA, deriving the mean, principal-eigenvector loading solutions, isotropic residual variance, and their variance interpretation. It explains rotational non-identifiability, covariance behavior in retained and discarded directions, numerical and EM considerations, and the reduction to ordinary Gaussian maximum likelihood when no dimensionality reduction is used. It also describes posterior latent inference and reconstruction, the zero-noise PCA limit, PPCA's reduced parameter complexity and degrees of freedom, and introduces EM as an iterative alternative useful for high-dimensional, factor-analysis, and missing-data settings.

nodes.title: 12.2.2 EM algorithm for peA
nodes.summary: The text explains PPCA's parameter efficiency and covariance degrees of freedom, including its limiting cases of full and isotropic covariance. It derives and describes EM estimation for PPCA, including posterior sufficient statistics, parameter updates, computational advantages over covariance eigendecomposition, online implementation, and principled treatment of missing data. It then presents the zero-noise limit recovering an EM form of standard PCA, interprets its projection and subspace-update steps through a spring-and-rod analogy, and introduces Bayesian PCA's issue of selecting latent dimensionality using application needs or gaps in the eigenvalue spectrum. Figures and related exercises are also referenced.

nodes.title: 12.2.3 Bayesian peA
nodes.summary: The text explains the EM algorithm for probabilistic PCA through a spring-and-rod analogy and figures showing projection, missing-data handling, and iterative subspace updates. It then discusses selecting latent dimensionality using eigenvalue gaps, cross-validation, variational Bayesian model selection, and an ARD-based Bayesian PCA approach that prunes unnecessary dimensions through precision hyperparameters. It presents the marginal-likelihood and Laplace-approximation updates, explains the resulting range of effective model dimensionalities and computational trade-offs, illustrates Gibbs-sampling behavior, notes extensions to fully Bayesian PCA, and introduces factor analysis as a related model.

nodes.title: 12.2.4 Factor analysis
nodes.summary: The text develops Bayesian PCA using Laplace and Gibbs approximations, explaining its EM updates, dimensionality selection, and illustrative posterior behavior. It then introduces factor analysis as a related linear-Gaussian latent-variable model with diagonal noise covariance, explains its covariance interpretation, rotational indeterminacy, likelihood and EM estimation equations, computational advantages, Bayesian extension, and transformation behavior. Finally, it begins kernel PCA, showing how PCA can be reformulated using centered-data scalar products and generalized through nonlinear feature-space mappings and kernel substitution.

The section develops probabilistic PCA as a constrained Gaussian latent-variable model equivalent to PCA under maximum likelihood, covering its generative and marginal distributions, parameter estimates, posterior inference, reconstruction, rotational ambiguity, covariance and parameter-count interpretations, and zero-noise connection to ordinary PCA. It presents EM estimation, including sufficient statistics, updates, computational and online advantages, missing-data handling, and geometric intuition. It then addresses latent-dimensionality selection through eigenvalue methods, cross-validation, Bayesian PCA, ARD pruning, Laplace and Gibbs approximations, and fully Bayesian extensions. The section also introduces factor analysis, detailing its diagonal-noise covariance model, estimation, identifiability, Bayesian treatment, and computational properties, before beginning kernel PCA through kernelized inner products and nonlinear feature mappings.

nodes.title: 12.3. Kernel peA
nodes.summary: The text briefly completes the discussion of factor analysis, noting efficient M-step computation, Bayesian extensions, and its different scaling behavior compared with PCA and probabilistic PCA. It then develops kernel PCA by expressing feature-space PCA entirely through kernel evaluations: feature-space eigenvectors are expanded over mapped training samples, solved via the Gram-matrix eigenproblem, normalized appropriately, and used to compute projections. It explains implicit feature-space centering, recovery of ordinary PCA with a linear kernel, the possible increase in nonlinear component count, and a Gaussian-kernel clustering example. Finally, it discusses the computational cost of the N by N kernel matrix and the difficulty of reconstructing original-space pre-images from truncated feature-space projections.

nodes.title: 12.4. Nonlinear Latent Variable Models
12.4.1 Independent component analysis
nodes.summary: The section introduces nonlinear and non-Gaussian extensions of linear-Gaussian latent-variable models, noting that nonlinear transformations of Gaussian references can generate general densities. It then presents ICA, in which observed variables are linear mixtures of independent, non-Gaussian latent components, motivating the model through blind separation of mixed speech signals. The mixing parameters are estimated by likelihood optimization, but identifiability requires non-Gaussian latent distributions because Gaussian models cannot distinguish rotations of latent space and uncorrelated components are not necessarily independent. Heavy-tailed distributions are commonly used. Probabilistic ICA motivates extensions such as independent factor analysis, which supports unequal latent and observed dimensions, noise, Gaussian-mixture latent distributions, EM learning, and variational reconstruction. The text concludes by pointing to the broad ICA literature and introducing autoassociative neural networks.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 Autoassociative neural networks
outputs
nodes.summary: The text explains autoassociative neural networks for unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Two-layer networks, even with nonlinear hidden units, achieve the same solution as linear PCA, while deeper networks can learn nonlinear latent manifolds at the cost of difficult nonconvex optimization and a preselected latent dimension. It then surveys nonlinear-manifold modeling using local PCA mixtures, probabilistic PCA mixtures and their Bayesian, factor-analysis, and hierarchical variants, before introducing principal curves as a single nonlinear generalization of PCA.

The section discusses ICA and autoassociative neural networks for latent-variable modeling and dimensionality reduction. It explains why Gaussian linear latent-variable models cannot identify independent components because of rotational ambiguity and because uncorrelatedness does not imply independence, motivating heavy-tailed non-Gaussian priors, likelihood-based ICA, and extensions such as independent factor analysis learned with EM and variational inference. It then introduces autoassociative networks, noting that shallow models reproduce PCA while deeper networks can represent nonlinear manifolds at the cost of nonconvex optimization and a prespecified latent dimension, and surveys mixture-based local and probabilistic PCA methods, their Bayesian, factor-analysis, and hierarchical variants, and principal curves.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 Modelling nonlinear manifolds
nodes.summary: The text surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold-learning methods. It discusses nonlinear neural-network PCA and its optimization drawbacks; piecewise-linear models, probabilistic PCA mixtures, factor analysers, and hierarchical mixtures; principal curves and surfaces; MDS, LLE, and Isomap; latent trait models and exponential-family extensions; density networks and their Monte Carlo limitations; and GTM as an efficient probabilistic nonlinear manifold model, including its relation to SOMs, extensions, and geometric visualization tools. It concludes with exercises covering PCA eigenvector proofs and optimization, Gaussian transformations, probabilistic PCA graphical and marginal/posterior distributions, maximum-likelihood mean estimation, limiting posterior behavior, and optimal reconstruction.

This section presents nonlinear and non-Gaussian latent-variable approaches, beginning with ICA and its identifiability, likelihood learning, heavy-tailed priors, and probabilistic extensions. It then covers autoassociative neural networks and related mixture, factor-analysis, Bayesian, hierarchical, and principal-curve methods for dimensionality reduction. A broader survey treats nonlinear manifold learning through neural networks, MDS, LLE, Isomap, latent-trait and exponential-family models, density networks, and GTM, including computational, probabilistic, geometric, and visualization aspects. Exercises reinforce PCA, Gaussian transformations, probabilistic PCA inference, estimation, posterior limits, and reconstruction.

nodes.title: 12.3 (*) Verify that the eigenvectors defined by (12.30) are normalized to unit length, assuming that the eigenvectors Vi have unit length.
nodes.summary: This text presents exercises on probabilistic PCA and related Gaussian results. It covers eigenvector normalization and parameter-equivalent latent Gaussian reparameterizations; affine transformations of Gaussian variables and their dimensional cases; graphical-model independence; derivations of the probabilistic PCA marginal and posterior distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean; the zero-noise connection to orthogonal PCA projection; the shrinkage effect of positive noise; and the least-squares optimal reconstruction formula.

nodes.title: 12.12 (* *) For (Y2 > 0 show that the posterior mean in the probabilistic PCA model is shifted towards the origin relative to the orthogonal projection.
nodes.summary: The text introduces exercises on the eigenvector solution of probabilistic PCA, including normalization and equivalence under general Gaussian latent distributions; affine transformations of Gaussian variables and their dimensional cases; graphical-model independence structure; derivations of the probabilistic PCA marginal and posterior distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean; and comparisons between probabilistic PCA posterior means, conventional PCA projections, noise-induced shrinkage toward the origin, and least-squares-optimal reconstruction.

nodes.title: 12.13 (* *) Show that the optimal reconstruction of a data point under probabilistic PCA, according to the least squares projection cost of conventional PCA, is given by
nodes.summary: This text presents exercises on probabilistic PCA and factor analysis. The problems cover eigenvector normalization and covariance parameter counts; invariance to general Gaussian latent parameterizations and latent-space rotations; affine transformations and Gaussian marginal and posterior derivations; graphical-model independence; maximum-likelihood estimation of the mean and verification of its unique maximum; the relationship between probabilistic PCA and conventional PCA, including zero-noise projections, noise-induced shrinkage, and least-squares reconstruction; derivation of EM updates for probabilistic PCA and factor analysis; handling missing data in probabilistic PCA; and derivation of PCA reconstruction updates and factor-analysis parameter and E-step formulas.

nodes.title: 12.19 (**) IIiI!I Show that the factor analysis model described in Section 12.2.4 is invariant under rotations of the latent space coordinates.
nodes.summary: Exercises 12.14–12.29 cover parameter counting and EM derivations for probabilistic PCA and factor analysis, including missing-data PCA, least-squares interpretations, latent-space rotational invariance, mean estimation, and graphical models for PCA mixtures. They also address EM for Student's t-distributions, transformation and covariance properties of linear-Gaussian latent-variable models, equivalence results for PCA eigenproblems, recovery of linear PCA from kernel PCA, density transformations under nonlinear changes of variables, and the distinction between independence and zero correlation.

nodes.title: 13 Sequential Data
13.1. Markov Models
nodes.summary: The text develops Markov and state-space approaches to sequential data. It contrasts i.i.d. models with first- and higher-order Markov chains, explains their factorized joint distributions and conditional-independence properties, and discusses stationary chains, parameter growth, autoregressive linear-Gaussian models, and neural-network tapped delay lines. It then introduces state-space models with Markov latent variables and conditionally generated observations, showing that they can capture dependencies on arbitrarily long observation histories while remaining tractable. Hidden Markov models are presented as the discrete-latent special case and as temporally coupled mixture models, with applications in speech, language, handwriting, and biological sequences; their multinomial latent states are encoded one-of-K and governed by a row-normalized transition matrix. Linear dynamical systems are identified as the Gaussian counterpart.

nodes.title: 13.2. Hidden Markov Models
13.2.1 Maximum likelihood for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains HMMs’ ability to model local temporal warping, illustrated by handwritten digits and speech, while noting that a left-to-right model strongly penalizes reversed sequences. It then develops maximum-likelihood HMM training: direct marginalization over K^N latent paths is exponential and direct optimization lacks closed-form solutions, motivating EM. The E step computes state and successive-state posterior marginals, while the M step updates initial and transition probabilities by normalized expected counts and emission parameters by weighted maximum likelihood, including Gaussian and multinomial examples and initialization considerations. Finally, it introduces the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm as the efficient exact method for obtaining the required posterior marginals.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 The forward-backward algorithm
nodes.summary: The text completes the EM treatment of hidden Markov models by giving emission-parameter updates for Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli observations, discussing initialization, and deriving the forward-backward algorithm for the E step. It defines forward and backward messages, derives their recursions and boundary conditions, computes state and transition posteriors, explains likelihood evaluation and its O(K²N) efficiency, and summarizes the full EM training procedure and practical issues such as sequence length, multiple sequences, and left-to-right models. It also derives real-time predictive distributions, notes applicability to arbitrary emission distributions, describes regularized and variational Bayesian extensions, and begins showing that the same recursions follow from the sum-product algorithm on a simplified factor graph.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 The sum-product algorithm for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text extends the HMM discussion from parameter estimation to regularized and fully Bayesian methods, then derives the forward-backward alpha and beta recursions using sum-product message passing on a simplified factor graph. It shows how message products produce hidden-state marginals and related joint probabilities. Finally, it explains numerical underflow in unscaled recursions and introduces normalized forward variables and conditional-likelihood scaling factors to maintain stable computations.

nodes.title: 13.2.4 Scaling factors
nodes.summary: The text connects the hidden Markov model forward-backward recursions to sum-product message passing, showing how alpha, beta, state marginals, and pairwise marginals arise from factor-graph messages. It then addresses numerical underflow through normalized alpha and beta variables and scaling factors, derives their recursions, explains likelihood and marginal recovery, and contrasts the standard alpha-beta method with an alpha-gamma alternative. Finally, it introduces the Viterbi algorithm as max-sum message passing for finding the most probable entire hidden-state sequence, emphasizing its distinction from independently maximizing marginals, its use of log probabilities, and its linear computational complexity.

nodes.title: 13.2.5 The Viterbi algorithm
nodes.summary: The text contrasts the alpha-gamma and standard alpha-beta forward-backward recursions, then introduces the Viterbi algorithm for finding the globally most probable HMM state sequence rather than independently most probable states. It derives the log-domain max-sum recursion, initialization, probabilistic interpretation, predecessor storage, and backtracking procedure, explains its dynamic-programming efficiency over exponentially many lattice paths, and concludes with HMM extensions, especially discriminative rather than maximum-likelihood training for sequence classification using a cross-entropy objective based on class-specific model likelihoods and priors.

nodes.title: 13.2.6 Extensions of the hidden Markov model
nodes.summary: The text explains the dynamic-programming intuition behind Viterbi decoding and surveys major HMM extensions: discriminative class-based training, explicit state-duration modelling, autoregressive observations, input-output conditioning, and factorial latent chains. It describes their motivations, probabilistic independence properties, training and inference procedures, computational costs, and the use of variational methods when exact inference is impractical. It then introduces linear dynamical systems through noisy sensing of a time-varying quantity, motivating adaptive and weighted averaging of recent observations.

This section develops hidden Markov models as discrete-state sequential models and temporally dependent mixture models, specifying their initial, transition, and emission distributions, joint probability, graphical and trellis representations, applications, and alternative emission families. It explains maximum-likelihood learning with EM and the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm, including posterior calculations, likelihood evaluation, predictive inference, initialization, multiple-sequence and model-structure considerations, sum-product interpretation, and numerical scaling. It then presents Viterbi max-sum decoding for the most probable complete state path, discusses discriminative, regularized, and Bayesian training, and surveys extensions involving duration, autoregression, inputs, factorial state structures, and variational inference, before motivating linear dynamical systems.

nodes.title: 13.3. Linear Dynamical Systems
13.3.1 Inference in LDS
nodes.summary: The text develops LDS inference using Gaussian sum-product message passing, deriving the Kalman filtering recursions for predicted and updated state means, covariances, gains, and likelihood normalization constants, including initialization. It explains filtering as prediction followed by observation-based correction, discusses limiting noise regimes, and illustrates tracking with figures. It then introduces Kalman smoothing, which combines forward filtering with backward messages to incorporate all observations, derives the smoothed mean and covariance recursions, and gives the Gaussian pairwise posterior and cross-covariance needed for EM parameter learning.

nodes.title: 13.3.2 Learning in LDS
nodes.summary: The text derives EM-based maximum-likelihood learning for an LDS by computing posterior state moments in the E step and maximizing the expected complete-data log likelihood in the M step, yielding updates for the initial-state mean and covariance, transition matrix and noise covariance, and emission matrix and noise covariance. It notes straightforward MAP and approximate Bayesian extensions. It then discusses LDS extensions: Gaussian-mixture initial states remain tractable, mixture emissions cause exponential posterior growth, and non-linear or non-Gaussian models require approximate or sampling-based inference. Switching state-space models combine continuous LDS chains with a discrete switching chain and can be handled approximately by variational methods, while switching among discrete chains yields switching HMMs.

nodes.title: 13.3.3 Extensions of LDS
nodes.summary: The text discusses maximum-likelihood, MAP, and fully Bayesian parameter learning for linear dynamical systems, then surveys extensions. Gaussian-mixture initial states remain tractable, whereas mixture emissions cause exponential posterior growth. More general non-linear-Gaussian models require deterministic approximations, sampling, or linearization via the extended Kalman filter. It also introduces switching state space models, which combine continuous LDS chains with a discrete switching HMM; although exact inference is intractable, variational forward-backward methods are efficient, and an all-discrete version is the switching hidden Markov model.

nodes.title: 13.3.4 Particle filters
nodes.summary: The text develops particle filtering as a sequential Monte Carlo method for non-linear or non-Gaussian dynamical systems. It derives a weighted-sample approximation to p(z_n|X_n), with particles sampled from the predictive distribution and weights determined by the observation likelihood. The posterior at the next time step is represented as a mixture of transition distributions, from which particles are sampled and then reweighted using the new observation. The derivation relies on graph-based conditional independences established by d-separation. Alternative names for the method are listed, and an exercise asks readers to verify related Markov-model independences using d-separation.

This section introduces linear dynamical systems as linear-Gaussian state-space models for tracking changing latent quantities observed with noise, establishes their relationship to HMMs and continuous latent-variable models, and gives their Gaussian transition, emission, and initial-state formulations. It develops efficient Kalman filtering and Kalman smoothing inference, including state and pairwise posterior moments, and explains why Gaussian closure permits tractable message passing while mixtures and more general models may not. It derives EM parameter-learning updates, mentions MAP and Bayesian extensions, surveys mixture, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and switching-state-space generalizations, and concludes with particle filtering for difficult dynamical systems using weighted sequential Monte Carlo.

nodes.title: 13.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text derives the particle filter's predictive distribution as a weighted mixture of state-transition distributions using Bayes' theorem and d-separation-based conditional independences. It explains particle filtering as weighted-particle representation, predictive sampling, and reweighting using the next observation; gives its alternative names and illustrates the process in Figure 13.23. The exercises cover d-separation and probability-rule proofs of first- and second-order Markov properties, the absence of finite-order Markov structure in observed state-space data, and maximum-likelihood learning of parametric emission-model parameters.

nodes.title: 13.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents a schematic particle-filter operation and a set of exercises on Markov and higher-order Markov conditional independences, d-separation, hidden Markov model EM learning, constrained updates for initial and transition probabilities, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emissions, persistence of zero parameters, factor-graph posterior derivations, and training HMMs on multiple independent sequences.

nodes.title: 13.8 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on verifying and deriving hidden Markov model EM updates for initial and transition probabilities and for Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emissions; proving preservation of zero parameters; establishing HMM conditional independences through d-separation and probability rules; deriving pairwise latent-state posteriors via factor-graph sum-product messages; and extending EM training to multiple independent observation sequences using separate forward-backward computations and aggregate parameter re-estimation.

nodes.title: 13.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 13.5–13.16 develop and verify HMM inference and learning results. They derive EM updates for initial, transition, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emission parameters; examine zero-parameter persistence and training over multiple independent sequences; verify HMM conditional independences through d-separation and probability rules; connect forward, backward, and pairwise posterior quantities to factor-graph message passing; derive rescaled marginal formulas; and obtain the Viterbi forward recursion from the joint distribution using logarithms and maximization.

nodes.title: 13.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents multi-sequence Baum–Welch parameter re-estimation formulas, including Gaussian emission means, and lists exercises covering factor-graph interpretations of HMM alpha and beta messages, rescaled marginals, a direct Viterbi derivation, input-output HMM factorization and inference, Gaussian MAP sequences in linear dynamical systems, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing identities, affine-offset extensions of linear-Gaussian models through state augmentation, and the reduction of Kalman filtering for independent observations to single-Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimation.

nodes.title: 13.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sequential-data methods, covering recursion initialization, factor-graph representations and forward-backward inference for input-output hidden Markov models, equivalence of marginal and joint posterior maximization in Gaussian linear dynamical systems, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing equations using Gaussian and matrix identities, augmentation of linear Gaussian models with constant offsets, and the reduction of Kalman filtering for independent observations to maximum-likelihood estimation of a Gaussian mean. The final exercise is only partially included.

nodes.title: 13.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sequential-data models, covering recursion initialization, factor-graph representations and forward-backward inference for input-output hidden Markov models, Gaussian posterior maximization, derivations of Kalman filter and smoother equations, matrix-identity manipulations, affine extensions of linear dynamical systems, connections between Kalman filtering and Gaussian maximum likelihood and probabilistic PCA, noiseless and constant-state limiting cases, pairwise state posteriors and covariances, and verification of EM M-step updates for initial, transition, and emission parameters.

This section introduces stationary sequential-data modeling as an alternative to i.i.d. assumptions and develops finite-memory Markov and state-space approaches for prediction and inference. It covers Markov chains and autoregressive models, then treats hidden Markov models in detail, including their probabilistic structure, applications, forward-backward and Baum-Welch EM learning, Viterbi decoding, numerical methods, multi-sequence training, and major extensions. It next develops linear dynamical systems as continuous linear-Gaussian state-space models, with Kalman filtering, smoothing, EM, Bayesian and nonlinear generalizations, and particle filtering for harder systems. Extensive exercises derive and verify the associated conditional independences, message-passing and posterior formulas, parameter updates, decoding recursions, input-output and affine models, and connections to Gaussian estimation and probabilistic PCA.

nodes.title: 14 Combining Models
14.1. Bayesian Model Averaging
nodes.summary: The text introduces model combination through input-dependent selection, using decision trees as hard-selection examples and mixtures of experts as probabilistic soft-selection models. It distinguishes this approach from Bayesian model averaging: mixture models can assign different data points to different components, whereas Bayesian averaging assumes one candidate model generated the whole data set and updates uncertainty over that model as more data arrive. The distinction extends to predictive and conditional distributions. It then introduces committees, which average predictions from several models, motivated by the bias-variance decomposition of prediction error.

nodes.title: 14.2. Committees
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging, explaining their latent-variable and whole-data-set interpretations and noting that the distinction also applies to predictive and conditional distributions. It then presents committees, especially bootstrap aggregation, as averages of multiple model predictions that reduce variance; derives the individual and committee errors and shows the ideal 1/M reduction under zero-mean uncorrelated errors, while noting that correlated errors limit practical gains. Finally, it introduces boosting and AdaBoost, in which weak classifiers are trained sequentially on performance-weighted data, with misclassified examples emphasized and the final predictions combined by weighted voting.

nodes.title: 14.3. Boosting
14.3.1 Minimizing exponential error
nodes.summary: AdaBoost combines sequentially trained base classifiers, assigning higher training weights to repeatedly misclassified examples and larger ensemble coefficients to classifiers with lower weighted error. The text illustrates this process with decision stumps and explains it as stagewise minimization of an exponential loss. Holding earlier models fixed leads to the weighted-error objective, the coefficient formula, and the standard data-weight update; the final prediction is the sign of the weighted classifier sum. Finally, minimizing the expected exponential loss over arbitrary functions yields a half-log posterior-odds decision function.

nodes.title: 14.3.2 Error functions for boosting
nodes.summary: The text completes the derivation of AdaBoost’s classifier coefficient, data-weight update, and final sign-based prediction rule. It interprets exponential-loss minimization as approximation of half the log posterior odds, compares exponential loss with cross-entropy, hinge, and misclassification losses, and discusses its strong outlier sensitivity, lack of a direct probabilistic interpretation, and limited multiclass applicability. The additive-model viewpoint motivates alternative boosting losses, multiclass methods, and regression boosting using squared or more robust absolute error. The text then introduces tree-based models, which partition input space into axis-aligned regions selected by binary-tree traversal, focusing on CART and briefly noting ID3 and C4.5.

The section motivates boosting as a way to overcome the limited gains of averaging correlated models and presents AdaBoost, which sequentially trains weak classifiers on adaptively reweighted data, emphasizes misclassified examples, assigns larger coefficients to more accurate classifiers, and combines their predictions by weighted voting. It derives the method as stagewise exponential-loss minimization, relates the optimum to posterior log odds, compares exponential loss with other classification losses and discusses its drawbacks, and surveys extensions to multiclass and regression settings. The section concludes by introducing decision-tree base models, particularly CART, along with ID3 and C4.5.

nodes.title: 14.4. Tree-based Models
nodes.summary: The text contrasts squared and absolute loss, noting the robustness of absolute deviation to outliers, then introduces CART and related tree-based models as interpretable systems that recursively partition input space with hard, axis-aligned binary splits and assign simple predictive models to leaves. It explains regression-tree fitting, greedy split selection, large-tree growth and complexity-penalized pruning, followed by classification criteria based on cross-entropy and the Gini index. It also discusses tree interpretability and weaknesses, including instability, inefficient axis-aligned boundaries, hard assignments, and discontinuous regression predictions. Finally, it motivates conditional mixture models and hierarchical mixtures of experts as probabilistic extensions using soft, multivariable splits and conditional leaf models.

nodes.title: 14.5. Conditional Mixture Models
14.5.1 Mixtures of linear regression models
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional mixture models and their extensions to mixtures and hierarchical mixtures of experts, then develops a mixture of linear regression models with Gaussian component noise. It formulates the likelihood and latent-variable complete-data likelihood, derives the EM algorithm—including responsibilities, mixing-coefficient updates, responsibility-weighted least-squares regression updates, and the shared precision update—and discusses a two-line synthetic example. Although the mixture improves likelihood and models multimodality better than a single regression, fixed mixing coefficients cause unwanted bimodal predictions across all inputs; input-dependent coefficients motivate mixture density networks and hierarchical mixtures of experts. The excerpt then begins mixtures of logistic regression models, giving their conditional distribution and parameterization, with the data likelihood only introduced before the text ends.

nodes.title: 14.5.2 Mixtures of logistic models
nodes.summary: The text presents mixtures of conditional models. It first illustrates EM fitting of two linear regressions, including component responsibilities and the superior bimodal predictive density and likelihood obtained over a single linear regression. It then derives EM for mixtures of logistic regressions: the mixture likelihood, latent component indicators, E-step responsibilities, expected complete-data log likelihood, mixing-weight update, and independent weighted logistic-regression M-step updates solved by IRLS using the stated gradient and Hessian. The method extends to multiclass softmax mixtures. Finally, it introduces mixtures of experts, in which input-dependent gating functions determine the mixing coefficients so different expert models can specialize in different regions of input space.

nodes.title: 14.5.3 Mixtures of experts
nodes.summary: The text derives the EM updates for mixtures of logistic regression models: mixing weights have a responsibility average update, while each component’s logistic-regression parameters are independently optimized by weighted IRLS using responsibilities as data weights. It illustrates the benefit over a single logistic classifier and notes extension to softmax mixtures. It then introduces mixtures of experts with input-dependent gating functions, explains linear gating and expert models, and describes the more flexible hierarchical mixture of experts, its EM/IRLS training, relation to decision trees and mixture density networks, and their respective advantages. Finally, it lists exercises on Bayesian model averaging and latent variables, committee error derivations, Jensen’s inequality and convex losses, and conditions for weighted committee predictions to remain within member prediction bounds.

This section explains how conditional mixture models overcome the hard, axis-aligned, unstable, and discontinuous nature of standard decision trees. It develops Gaussian mixtures of linear regressions and mixtures of logistic or softmax models, deriving their EM training procedures with responsibilities, mixing-weight updates, and weighted regression or IRLS parameter updates, and illustrates their advantages and limitations. It then introduces mixtures of experts with input-dependent gating and hierarchical mixtures of experts, relating them to decision trees and mixture density networks. Exercises address Bayesian model averaging, latent variables, committee errors, Jensen’s inequality, convex losses, and bounds on weighted committee predictions.

nodes.title: 14.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of combining models by describing the flexible, nonlinear soft partitions of mixture density networks, then presents exercises on marginalizing latent variables and model uncertainty in predictive distributions, distinguishing Bayesian model averaging from within-model latent-variable marginalization, deriving and interpreting committee-model error relationships, proving that committee averaging does not increase expected error via Jensen’s inequality, generalizing this to convex loss functions, and establishing that weighted committee predictions remain within the members’ prediction range exactly when the weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

nodes.title: 14.3 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of mixture density networks by noting their shared hidden units and flexible, nonlinear soft input-space partitions, then presents exercises on Bayesian averaging versus latent variables, committee-model error derivations, Jensen’s inequality and the superiority of committee averaging for convex errors, and the conditions under which unequally weighted committee predictions remain within the range of their members.

nodes.title: 14.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes a discussion of mixture density networks, emphasizing that shared hidden units generate component densities and mixing coefficients and that their input-space partitions are soft, non-axis-aligned, and nonlinear. It then presents exercises on marginalizing latent variables and model indices in Bayesian model prediction, distinguishing model averaging from within-model latent variables, deriving and comparing committee-model errors through Jensen's inequality, generalizing the comparison to arbitrary convex error functions, and proving that bounded unequally weighted committee predictions require nonnegative weights summing to one.

nodes.title: 14.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.15 ask for derivations and verifications concerning AdaBoost error minimization and updates, variational minimization of exponential loss, the lack of a normalized probabilistic interpretation for that loss, residual fitting in boosted least-squares models, and the mean as the least-squares-optimal constant prediction. They also compare tree impurity and classification measures, extend mixture linear regression to vector targets, verify its complete-data likelihood, derive EM mixing-coefficient updates using Lagrange multipliers, and establish that its conditional-mean prediction is a weighted combination of component means, with limitations for multimodal distributions.

nodes.title: 14.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.15 cover derivations and verifications involving AdaBoost error minimization, variational optimization of exponential loss, the probabilistic interpretation of exponential loss, boosting with squared-error residuals, and the mean as the least-squares predictor. They also compare tree criteria using misclassification rate, cross-entropy, and Gini index; extend mixture-of-linear-regression models to vector targets; verify their complete-data likelihood; derive EM mixing-coefficient updates with Lagrange multipliers; and establish that their conditional-mean prediction is a weighted combination of component means that can be inadequate for multimodal distributions.

nodes.title: 14.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The exercises cover derivations and verification of AdaBoost updates and its variational interpretation, the lack of a normalized probabilistic model for its exponential loss, residual fitting in boosting with squared error, and the mean as the optimal constant squared-error prediction. They also compare tree impurity measures using misclassification rate, cross-entropy, and Gini index, extend mixture-of-linear-regression models to vector targets, verify their complete-data likelihood, derive EM mixing-coefficient updates via Lagrange multipliers, and analyze conditional-mean predictions for mixtures, including their limitations for multimodal distributions.

nodes.title: 14.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The exercises cover derivations and properties of boosting, including the AdaBoost coefficient update, variational minimization of exponential loss, the lack of a corresponding normalized probabilistic model, residual fitting for squared-error boosting, and the mean as the optimal constant predictor. They compare classification trees using misclassification rate, cross-entropy, and Gini index. The remaining problems develop mixture models: extending linear regression mixtures to vector targets, deriving complete-data likelihoods and EM mixing-coefficient updates, analyzing conditional-mean predictions, extending logistic mixtures to multiclass softmax mixtures, and proving when hierarchical mixtures can or cannot be reduced to single-level mixtures, particularly under linear classification gating functions.

nodes.title: 14.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents two exercises: deriving EM for a mixture of softmax classifiers, and analyzing hierarchical conditional mixtures. Hierarchical mixtures collapse to ordinary mixtures when their mixing coefficients are arbitrary functions of the input, but this equivalence generally fails when both levels are restricted to linear logistic or softmax gating models, as demonstrated by a two-level-to-three-component counterexample.

This section surveys methods for combining models, contrasting Bayesian model averaging with input-dependent mixture models and prediction committees. It explains bagging and committee error reduction, then develops AdaBoost as sequential, weighted weak-learner training derived from exponential-loss minimization, with classification, regression, and multiclass extensions. It presents CART and related decision trees, their fitting, pruning, impurity criteria, interpretability, and limitations, and then introduces conditional mixtures, mixtures of experts, hierarchical experts, and mixture density networks as softer and more flexible alternatives. Exercises reinforce the theoretical derivations, loss functions, error bounds, tree criteria, EM algorithms, mixture predictions, and equivalence properties of hierarchical models.

Appendix C covers dimensionality reduction and latent-variable modeling, from classical, high-dimensional, probabilistic, kernel, nonlinear, and manifold-learning forms of PCA through factor analysis and ICA, including theory, inference, computation, Bayesian methods, reconstruction, identifiability, and extensive exercises. It then develops sequential-data models, including Markov and autoregressive processes, hidden Markov models, linear dynamical systems, Kalman methods, EM, smoothing, and particle filtering. Finally, it surveys model combination through Bayesian averaging, committees, bagging, AdaBoost, decision trees, mixtures of experts, hierarchical experts, and mixture density networks, together with their algorithms, interpretations, theoretical properties, and exercises.

structure.summary: The section is a comprehensive contents overview of a pattern-recognition and machine-learning text. It covers foundational probability, Bayesian inference, distributions, decision and information theory; statistical estimation, model selection, regularization, and dimensionality; core models including regression, classification, neural, kernel, graphical, mixture, and exponential-family models; latent-variable methods, dimensionality reduction, sequential and dynamical models, and ensemble learning. It also develops variational, message-passing, expectation-propagation, and Monte Carlo inference, with extensive theoretical and practical exercises, and concludes with appendices on the calculus of variations and Lagrange multipliers, references, and an index.

structure.title: Appendix A. Data Sets

nodes.title: Handwritten Digits
nodes.summary: The appendix briefly introduces the book's illustrative data sets and provides a website for their files and formats. It describes MNIST handwritten digits, including their NIST origin, train/test composition, writer separation, image preprocessing, example figure, and benchmark classification error rates. It then introduces the synthetic Oil Flow data set, explaining dual-energy gamma densitometry, why two attenuation measurements are needed to determine the three phase fractions, how the fractions are calculated from known absorption properties, and how low flow velocity produces stratified oil, water, and gas layers.

nodes.title: Oil Flow
nodes.summary: The text introduces a brief MNIST example caption, then describes the Oil Flow synthetic gamma-densitometry data set, including its physical motivation, three flow geometries, six-beam 12-dimensional noisy measurements, generation procedure, data splits, prediction uses, and manifold structure. It concludes with the 272-observation Old Faithful data set, recording eruption duration and waiting time and noting their predictive relationship.

nodes.title: Old Faithful
nodes.summary: The text describes the manifold structure of oil-and-water observations under homogeneous, annular, and laminar configurations, including photon-noise effects, nonlinearities, discontinuities, segmentation, and intersections. It then introduces the 272-observation Old Faithful data set of eruption durations and waiting times, noting the predictive relationship between them. Finally, it describes two recurring synthetic data sets: noisy sinusoidal regression data and a two-class Gaussian-mixture classification problem for which exact posterior probabilities and the optimal decision boundary are available.

nodes.title: Synthetic Data
nodes.summary: The text presents an Old Faithful eruption-duration plot and describes two synthetic data sets used throughout the book: a noisy sinusoidal regression set with uniformly sampled inputs and a two-class Gaussian-based classification set. It explains the corresponding visualizations, including the regression conditional distribution, classification posterior probabilities, and the optimal 0.5-posterior decision boundary.

structure.summary: This appendix introduces the book's illustrative data sets and their online file resources: MNIST handwritten digits, the synthetic Oil Flow gamma-densitometry data set and its physical, geometric, measurement, and manifold characteristics, and the Old Faithful eruption and waiting-time observations. It also presents recurring synthetic regression and classification data sets, including their generation, visualizations, posterior probabilities, and optimal decision boundary.

structure.title: Appendix B. Probability Distributions

nodes.title: Bernoulli
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces probability distributions from the exponential family and lists their main statistics. It then describes the Bernoulli distribution for a binary variable, giving its parameterization, probability mass function, expectation, variance, mode, and entropy, and noting that it is a one-observation binomial distribution whose parameter has a beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Beta
nodes.summary: The text introduces the beta and binomial probability distributions. It defines the beta distribution on [0,1], gives its density, mean, variance, and mode, and explains its parameter constraints, conjugacy to the Bernoulli distribution, interpretation as prior counts, boundary singularities, uniform special case, and relationship to the Dirichlet distribution. It then defines the binomial probability of m successes in N Bernoulli trials, provides its mean, variance, mode, and combinatorial coefficient with the definition of factorial, and notes its Bernoulli special case, Gaussian approximation for large N, and beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Binomial
nodes.summary: The text presents the beta, binomial, and Dirichlet probability distributions, giving their definitions, parameter constraints, densities, moments, variances, modes, and related formulas. It explains beta–Bernoulli and Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy, interprets parameters as effective observation counts, discusses boundary singularities and special cases, defines binomial coefficients and factorials, notes the Bernoulli and Gaussian approximations, and provides the Dirichlet normalization constant, covariance, expected log variables, entropy, and digamma-function notation.

nodes.title: Gamma
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gamma and Gaussian probability distributions, giving their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, expected log values, and entropies. It explains the Gamma distribution’s role as a conjugate prior for Gaussian precision and identifies the exponential special case. It then introduces the scalar Gaussian distribution, its parameters and properties, defines precision and standard deviation, describes its conjugate priors, and briefly extends the Gaussian to D-dimensional vectors with a mean vector and symmetric covariance matrix.

nodes.title: Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gamma, scalar and multivariate Gaussian, Gaussian-Gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, and Multinomial distributions. It gives their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, entropies, precision relationships, conjugate-prior roles, and key structural properties. It also provides Gaussian marginalization, conditioning, affine-transformation identities, partitioned-Gaussian formulas, and the Multinomial’s one-hot representation, moments, covariances, and entropy.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Gamma
nodes.summary: The text presents Gaussian marginal distributions, the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for Gaussian models with unknown means and precisions, their scalar equivalence, and the definition, moments, covariances, and entropy of a K-dimensional multinomial one-hot distribution.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Wishart
nodes.summary: The text gives the Gaussian marginal for a subset of variables, defines Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for Gaussian models with unknown means and precisions, notes their scalar equivalence, and introduces the one-hot multinomial distribution along with its probability, moments, covariances, and entropy.

nodes.title: Multinomial
nodes.summary: The text presents Gaussian marginal distributions and conjugate priors for Gaussian models: the Gaussian-Gamma for unknown univariate mean and precision, and the Gaussian-Wishart for unknown multivariate mean and precision, with the scalar case reducing to Gaussian-Gamma. It then introduces the multinomial distribution and its one-hot and count-based forms, constraints, moments, entropy, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. Finally, it clarifies the terminology linking normal and Gaussian distributions and begins describing Student’s t-distribution as a Gaussian with gamma-distributed precision integrated out.

nodes.title: Normal
nodes.summary: The text presents the multinomial distribution, its probability formula, parameter constraints, combinatorial coefficient, moments, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It then clarifies terminology for the normal/Gaussian, Gaussian-gamma, and Gaussian-Wishart distributions, and introduces Student’s t-distribution with its historical origin and derivation as a Gaussian whose precision has a gamma prior that is integrated out, yielding an infinite mixture.

nodes.title: Student’s t
nodes.summary: The text covers the multinomial distribution, including its probability formula, parameter constraints, combinatorial coefficient, moments, covariances, and Dirichlet conjugate prior; clarifies terminology for the normal/Gaussian distribution and related distributions; develops univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, their Gaussian-mixture interpretation, moments, mode, degrees of freedom, Cauchy special case, Mahalanobis-distance form, Gaussian limiting case, and robustness; and presents the uniform distribution’s density, moments, entropy, and interval-transformation property.

nodes.title: Uniform
nodes.summary: The text presents the univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, including their densities, parameters, moments, modes, degrees-of-freedom interpretation, Cauchy special case, Wishart-Gaussian construction, Mahalanobis distance, Gaussian limiting behavior, and robustness to outliers. It then defines the continuous uniform distribution on [a, b], gives its density, mean, variance, and entropy, and states the affine transformation from a standard uniform variable.

nodes.title: Von Mises
nodes.summary: The text presents the von Mises circular analogue of a Gaussian, defining its periodic density, Bessel-function normalization, angular interpretation, concentration parameter, and Gaussian approximation. It then defines the Wishart distribution as the multivariate Gaussian precision-matrix conjugate prior, giving its density and normalization, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter constraints, and reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

nodes.title: Wishart
nodes.summary: The text introduces the periodic von Mises distribution and the Wishart distribution. It gives the von Mises density, periodicity, interpretation of its location and concentration parameters, and its Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then presents the Wishart density and normalization, its mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter requirements and definitions, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

structure.summary: This appendix surveys major probability distributions and their key statistics, formulas, parameter constraints, special cases, approximations, transformations, and conjugate-prior relationships. It covers Bernoulli, beta, binomial, Dirichlet, Gamma, scalar and multivariate Gaussian, Gaussian-Gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, multinomial, Student’s t, uniform, von Mises, and Wishart distributions, including Gaussian marginalization and conditioning identities, mixture constructions, precision representations, circular and multivariate extensions, factorial and normalization functions, entropy and expected-log formulas, and interpretations of parameters as counts, means, variances, concentrations, or precisions.

structure.title: Appendix C. Properties of Matrices

nodes.title: Basic Matrix Identities
nodes.summary: The excerpt introduces an appendix of standard matrix and determinant properties, assuming basic linear algebra and valid dimensions and inverses. It defines matrix, identity, transpose, inverse, linear independence, rank, trace, and determinant notation; states transpose, inverse, trace-cyclicity, and determinant identities; presents computationally useful inverse formulas including a dimension-reducing identity, a special case, and the Woodbury identity; and briefly explains the computational contexts and verification methods for these results. The determinant discussion begins with its signed permutation-style expansion and is cut off at the end of the excerpt.

nodes.title: Traces and Determinants
nodes.summary: The text surveys key matrix properties and identities: inverse identities including a computational form, a special inverse relation, and the Woodbury identity; linear independence and matrix rank; trace and its cyclic property; determinant definitions, examples, multiplicative and inverse rules, Sylvester’s identity, and the rank-one determinant formula; and componentwise definitions of vector and matrix derivatives, culminating in the derivative of a linear scalar product.

nodes.title: Matrix Derivatives
nodes.summary: The text presents determinant properties, including the permutation definition, the 2×2 case, product and inverse rules, Sylvester’s identity, and the rank-one determinant formula. It then introduces vector and matrix derivatives and lists fundamental matrix-calculus, inverse, log-determinant, and trace derivative identities, concluding with the definition of the eigenvector equation.

nodes.title: Eigenvector Equation
nodes.summary: The text presents key matrix-derivative identities for products, inverses, determinants, and traces, then develops eigenvalue theory for square and especially symmetric matrices. It establishes real, orthonormal eigenvectors for real symmetric matrices; defines the orthogonal eigenvector matrix and explains its geometric interpretation as a rotation; derives eigendecomposition, inverse, determinant, and trace formulas; and concludes with the eigenvalue-based definitions of positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices, emphasizing that positive definiteness concerns the quadratic form rather than the signs of individual entries.

structure.summary: This appendix reviews standard matrix and determinant notation, identities, and computational formulas; covers linear independence, rank, traces, determinants, and their algebraic properties; introduces componentwise vector and matrix derivatives with fundamental product, inverse, determinant, log-determinant, and trace rules; and develops eigenvalue theory for symmetric matrices, including orthogonal eigendecomposition, inverse, determinant, and trace formulas. It concludes by defining positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices via quadratic forms and eigenvalues.

structure.title: Appendix D. Calculus of Variations
structure.summary: The appendix introduces functionals as mappings from functions to scalar values and presents the calculus of variations as the method for optimizing them, with examples involving curve length and entropy. It develops functional derivatives through arbitrary function perturbations, establishes that stationarity requires the derivative to vanish, and derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for integral functionals depending on a function and its derivative. An example produces a second-order differential equation solved with boundary conditions. It also covers the simpler case without derivative dependence, normalization constraints handled by Lagrange multipliers, and extension to multidimensional variables.

structure.title: Appendix E. Lagrange Multipliers
structure.summary: The appendix introduces Lagrange multipliers for finding extrema subject to equality or inequality constraints. It motivates the method geometrically: constraint gradients are normal to the constraint surface, and at a constrained extremum the objective gradient is parallel or antiparallel to that normal. For L(x, λ) = f(x) + λg(x), stationarity with respect to x and λ gives ∇f + λ∇g = 0 and g = 0, producing D + 1 equations for a D-dimensional variable. A quadratic maximization example yields (1/2, 1/2) with multiplier 1. Inequality constraints lead to inactive or active cases and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions g ≥ 0, λ ≥ 0, and λg = 0; minimization uses a sign-adjusted Lagrangian. The method is extended to multiple equality and inequality constraints, with complementary slackness for inequality multipliers, and to constrained functional derivatives.
